Family Photograph Archive — Completion and Future Handling
Recorded: January 1, 2028

ARCHIVE COMPLETION STATUS

The family photograph archive is complete as a preservation-scanning project. As of March 14, 2027, all 40 of the 40 archived family photographs had preservation scans; none remained undigitized. The final seven were scanned during Marcus Tanaka’s second one-time remote archive session. The originals remain in their archival sleeves. Completion of scanning does not mean that every photograph has a resolved identity, date, location, or occasion.

COLLECTION AND CONSERVATION HISTORY

- The working collection consists of 40 photographs: 32 dry photographs originally labeled P001–P032 and eight photographs that were in professional treatment.
- On August 9, 2024, the conservator returned the eight treated photographs with final condition notes. Six adhered corners were separated without additional image loss. Two mold-affected edges were cleaned and stabilized, with no central-image damage or loss to the central image. The eight returned prints were added to the same condition-based inventory as the 32 dry photographs.
- Before scanning the returned set, all 40 photographs were placed in archival sleeves and boxes.
- The treated set was scanned under temporary IDs P033–P040. All eight fronts and the three backs containing writing were captured. Unaltered TIFF masters and separate access copies were retained, two-person file and front-to-back verification was completed, and every original was returned immediately to its archival sleeve.
- The original envelopes, handwriting, provenance notes, condition notes, and existing no-removal boundaries remain part of the archive. Digital copies do not replace those sources.

PRESERVATION AND SOURCE RULES TO KEEP

- Keep each original in its archival sleeve/box and preserve its source position and associated envelope or provenance material.
- Keep front and back captures separate and preserve written backs. Use temporary/source IDs rather than guessed names, dates, places, or events in filenames or metadata.
- Retain visually similar photographs as separate sources when their backs, handwriting, or provenance differ. Photograph A and Photograph B were rescanned as distinct front/back pairs; their distinct backs are preserved, and they must not be merged or deduplicated merely because their fronts look similar.
- Preserve the condition-based inventory and the conservator’s notes. Do not clean, flatten, repair, mark, or otherwise alter originals as part of ordinary viewing or identification work.
- Use access copies for ordinary viewing or sharing. Keep archival masters unchanged and maintain the existing backup arrangement.
- The dry-residue no-removal boundary recorded in the final completion update remains in force: do not remove or disturb material under that boundary without appropriate conservation direction.

IDENTIFICATION AND UNCERTAINTY STATUS

Known and supported information must remain distinct from family recollection, approximation, or disagreement. Record uncertainty explicitly rather than converting it into fact. Unknown identity/date/location/occasion fields remain unknown unless new evidence supports a change.

Examples retained in the project history:

- P020–P032 remain unidentified wherever the family does not know the answer; do not infer from appearance, handwriting, context, or speculation.
- P023 remains disputed between Mom’s Austin/probably-2002 recollection and Marcus’s San Antonio/2004 recollection.
- P028 remains unidentified and undated.
- P027 is supported as the Portland garden outing in April 1994, showing Riley and Marcus Tanaka, with Mom’s labeled companion photograph “Marcus garden day - April 1994” as provenance. The exact day remains unresolved. Mom’s later calendar and nearby-album check found no note narrowing the day, and that absence is not evidence for any particular date.
- Any other unresolved identity, date, location, occasion, or source field remains as previously recorded in the inventory; the completion of scanning supplied no permission to infer new facts.

FUTURE HANDLING

Future identification review is optional and may occur only if the family chooses to revisit a particular item. There is no scheduled review, recurring call cadence, or automatic follow-up obligation.

If a future one-time review happens:

1. Start with the existing inventory, temporary ID, scan pair, envelope, handwriting, provenance, condition notes, and prior uncertainty—not a fresh guess from the image alone.
2. Review the original only under the existing handling and conservation boundaries; prefer access copies for initial viewing.
3. Record each participant’s statement in attributed language, separating confirmed information from possible, approximate, disputed, or unknown information.
4. Treat a new claim as an update only when it has identifiable supporting evidence. Preserve the prior entry and record what changed, why, when, and from which source.
5. If the review produces no new evidence, leave identity, date, location, occasion, and provenance fields unchanged.
6. Do not rename or reorganize archival masters solely because an identification is proposed. Keep source IDs stable and retain the audit trail.
7. If handling, residue, mold, adhesion, sleeve condition, or any other conservation concern arises, stop and obtain appropriate conservation guidance rather than experimenting on the original.

CLOSING STATE

Preservation scanning and basic archival housing are complete for all 40 photographs. The archive is stable, housed, and available for later, voluntary identification review. The durable rule is: preserve originals and provenance, keep source distinctions, use evidence before changing metadata, and allow unresolved questions to remain unresolved.

## Riley’s established personal-practice routine

- **Cadence:** one protected **Sunday watercolor block**, typically about **two hours**. It is personal restorative time, separate from Helio work, household logistics, relationship maintenance, and any make-up scheduling.
- **Established weekday:** **Sunday**, often in the morning, although the exact time can vary when a particular Sunday is needed for restaurant or household commitments.
- **Recurring subject/materials:** the practice repeatedly returns to quiet, observed subjects around **Cherrywood**—especially the kitchen/dining-corner window, interior light, counters, doorways, still lifes, shadows, and occasional Kibo studies. The established paper is usually **9 × 12-inch, 140-pound cold-press watercolor paper**; smaller studies have also used 6 × 8-inch paper. Recorded palettes include **ultramarine, burnt sienna, yellow ochre, and quinacridone rose**, depending on the study.
- **Recurring technique:** preserve the large value structure and keep cool and warm areas separate. In particular, Riley’s established method for a warm interior edge against a cool wash is **value separation rather than simply adding more orange**. Riley also tests wash timing and re-entry: waiting for the appropriate drying stage preserves a continuous cool shape and warm edge, while re-entering too soon breaks the wash. The practice favors changing one variable at a time when testing.
- **Storage/setup:** the permanent workspace is the naturally lit **Cherrywood dining-corner painting area**, with a painting table and narrow supply cabinet. Supplies can remain organized there rather than being cleared from shared surfaces. Finished, fully dry work is kept in **Riley’s private/Cherrywood watercolor portfolio**, as personal practice with no automatic sale, exhibition, or public-demonstration commitment.

## How January 2028 entries should fit Sam’s current cadence

The December 13, 2027 review established that the January rota could remain posted: all Mondays and the protected **Monday 6:30–9:30 p.m. shared block** remain intact, there is no recurring extra close, and Sam’s role terms are unchanged. The late notice—20 days rather than the guaranteed three weeks—was documented but **not treated as a reason to displace the rota or waive the guarantee**.

Therefore January entries should follow these boundaries:

1. **Keep every Monday 6:30–9:30 p.m. free of restaurant service and Helio work.** It is shared protected time, not default event coverage or a work catch-up block.
2. **Keep Sunday watercolor separate.** Do not move it into Monday, turn it into a relationship-maintenance obligation, or use it as make-up time for a missed dinner or rota conflict. Sunday remains flexible only as needed for restaurant realities.
3. **Use optional low-noise coffee or a Kibo walk only when both calendars allow.** These are additional, voluntary overlaps—not a second mandatory shared slot.

None changes the standing Monday/Sunday pattern.

## Decision

With the historical replay complete and showing **no semantic disagreement**, the Jan. 1, 2028 activation-recovery banner proposal may reach **bounded, non-customer-facing shadow**—but **not production**.

A clean replay satisfies the **replay → shadow** condition. It does not satisfy the **shadow → production** gate.

## Stage boundaries

- **Replay — complete:** historical evaluation only. It produced no customer-facing action, production write, audience/eligibility change, message, enrollment, or downstream effect.
- **Shadow — furthest permitted stage now:** isolated, nonproduction, shadow-only execution of the banner logic. It must preserve the existing contract and capture auditable evidence. It is not a release, activation, or customer exposure.
- **Production — still blocked:** no production connection, customer-facing banner, production approval, release, or authority change follows automatically from replay or clean shadow results.

## Intake contract that must remain explicit

1. **Customer action**
   - Display an activation-recovery/incomplete-setup banner only to a **qualifying human admin** when setup remains incomplete, entitlement is current and active, and no current Customer Success adoption or renewal work exists.
   - Eligibility is not outreach permission and does not create a reusable audience.

2. **Governed fields and meanings**
   - Entitlement.
   - Qualifying-human-admin status.
   - Active Customer Success adoption or renewal work.
   - Their existing meanings must remain unchanged. No new field—such as an inadequately governed manually maintained “renewal likelihood”—may be added without its own source owner, as-of rule, and freshness limit.

3. **Source and freshness**
   - For every governed field, retain the authoritative source owner, field-level as-of timestamp, consumer/evaluated-as-of timestamp, applicable freshness limit, and freshness result.
   - Use the unified, replay-verified UTC interpretation; feed-level recency cannot substitute for field-level freshness.
   - Missing, stale, unresolved, invalid, or conflicting state must not inherit a prior value.

4. **Fail-closed and suppression**
   - Missing, stale, or conflicting required state produces a visible field-specific hold.
   - Current active Customer Success adoption or renewal work suppresses the banner.
   - No unsafe positive qualification or revival of prior positive eligibility is allowed.

5. **Ownership**
   - Customer correction and incident stop: **Riley/the user**.
   - Engineering rollback: **Daniela**.
   - The intake must also document rollback/quarantine triggers, coordinated recovery steps, escalation ownership, and operator-visible hold reasons.

## Production approvals and evidence still required

### Evidence

Production requires a complete, reproducible evidence package tied to the exact build, configuration, input snapshot, transformation version, and replay window, including:

- Shadow coverage of the broader January population, all nine corrected fixtures, and the relevant missing-current-value, prior-true, stale, conflicting, invalid, deactivated-admin, unresolved-mapping, ordering, repeated-update, and malformed/out-of-order timestamp cases.

- Auditable record-level comparisons, complete coverage with classified omissions, deterministic rerun agreement, and zero unexplained cross-consumer mismatches.
- Zero prior-value inheritance, unsafe qualifications, unexplained omissions, or unresolved discrepancies.
- Passing fail-closed and suppression behavior, with visible field-level operator views showing source owner, as-of times, freshness result, and hold reason.
- Production-like validation of the corrected transformation path without live customer effects.

- **Riley/the user:** approval of the exact customer-action scope.

Decision — 2028-01-01

The historical replay is complete and found no semantic disagreement. Under the standing shared-state consumer admission gate, the proposal may currently progress no further than bounded, isolated, non-customer-facing shadow execution. Shadow must remain nonproduction and must not write, message, enroll, change an audience or eligibility state, create downstream effects, or alter field meanings or authority. The replay result does not authorize production connection, release, activation, or customer exposure.

Production remains blocked pending a complete evidence package tied to the exact build, configuration, versioned input snapshot/transformation, and replay or release window. The package must demonstrate complete and reproducible coverage, deterministic rerun and cross-consumer agreement, zero unexplained discrepancies or unsafe qualifications, correct field-level operator visibility, fail-closed and suppression behavior, monitoring and audit, failure-injection coverage, and tested coordinated rollback or fail-closed quarantine with named triggers, escalation, recovery, and rollback owners.

The following production approvals must still be separately recorded against that exact validated build and evidence:
- Riley/user approval of the exact customer-action scope.
- Daniela approval of production release controls and engineering rollback controls.
- Named production release owner approval of the exact build and replay/release window.
- Lifecycle/data-risk owner approval and review of the evidence package.

The intake must keep these fields and controls explicit:
- Customer action: display an activation-recovery banner only while setup remains incomplete, for a qualifying human admin, with current supported entitlement, and absent active Customer Success adoption or renewal work. This is not outreach permission, a reusable audience, or authority for another action; each display requires a fresh evaluation.
- Governed fields and unchanged meanings: entitlement, qualifying-human-admin status, and active Customer Success adoption or renewal work, plus the explicit incomplete-setup condition required by this proposal. No additional field may be introduced without its own meaning, authoritative source owner, as-of rule, and freshness limit.
- Source and freshness: authoritative source owner, field-level as-of timestamp, consumer/evaluated-as-of timestamp, applicable freshness limit, freshness result, and unified replay-verified UTC handling for every governed field. Feed-level recency must not replace field-level freshness.
- Fail-closed and suppression: missing, stale, unresolved, invalid, or conflicting required state produces a visible field-specific hold with no prior-value inheritance; current active Customer Success adoption or renewal work suppresses the banner.
- Ownership and controls: Riley/user owns customer correction and incident stop; Daniela owns engineering rollback. Rollback/quarantine triggers, coordinated recovery steps, escalation ownership, and operator-visible hold reasons must remain explicit.

The standing consumer boundary is unchanged: the shared-state feed currently has five production consumers, and this proposal is not authorized to become a sixth consumer. Clean replay or shadow does not itself grant production admission, new authority, semantic reinterpretation, or customer-facing release.

# Approved historical comparison: Helio Start in Q1 vs. Q2 2026

## The common rule

The quarterly handoff required each claim to name its denominator and use a complete, predeclared outcome window. For Helio Start, that meant admitted workspaces with complete day-90 windows, refund-adjusted collected cash, and account-level support effort. Evidence outside those scopes received no revenue or forecast credit.

## Q1 2026 — excluded because the operating gate was not board-ready

### Relevant Q1 facts, oldest to newest

- **February 13, 2026:** Helio Start had only one of the two required mature cohorts; exact cohort dates and certified source were missing.
- **February 24, 2026:** the second consecutive mature cohort was certified, satisfying the evidence condition to *consider* reopening a capped paid-acquisition proposal. The update nevertheless preserved the unresolved missing-cohort-dates limitation and `not board-ready` status.
- **March 3, 2026:** proposal-preparation authority was granted for a capped Q2 proposal, but Helio Start remained organic-only through March 31. No budget, paid traffic, acquisition authorization, pipeline target, forecast credit, or launch approval existed.
- **March 24, 2026:** the final Q1 claims review excluded Helio Start from the approved board operating-evidence section because the exact start and end dates for the cohorts—required by the January 6 readiness gate—were still missing.

### What the Q1 evidence meant for Q2 forecast credit

The two mature cohorts cleared an **operating/reconsideration gate only**: they allowed consideration, and later preparation, of a capped paid-acquisition proposal. They did **not** establish acquisition economics or authorize a commercial action. Therefore, they created **zero Q2 forecast credit**—and no paid traffic, approved budget, acquisition claim, pipeline treatment, launch approval, or revenue treatment.

**Q1 distinction:** the exclusion was driven primarily by an incomplete board-readiness/source-boundary condition—missing exact cohort dates—while the evidence itself was still explicitly non-commercial for forecasting purposes.

## Q2 2026 — excluded because the day-7 read was not a mature outcome

### Relevant Q2 facts, oldest to newest

- **May 25, 2026:** the fixed high-intent paid-search cohort completed its day-7 windows; 39 of 50 reached first integration. This was designated only as a predeclared leading operating read, not mature acquisition, scale, or forecast evidence.
- **June 12, 2026:** the source-completeness packet recorded the fixed 50-workspace cohort and the complete 39-of-50 day-7 read, while leaving the mature customer-outcome row incomplete pending day-90 windows for all 50 workspaces.
- **July 6, 2026:** complete day-90 paid-active status, refund-adjusted collected cash, and account-level support effort remained unavailable; consequently, no mature claim, lane closure, or board-readiness decision had been established.
- **July 10, 2026:** the final claims review excluded Helio Start from the approved Q2 section pending mature outcomes. The paid-pilot day-90 matter remained open separately, and no acquisition or forecast claim was added.

### Exactly what the day-7 result established

It established only that, within a **fixed denominator of 50 workspaces**, **39 reached first integration by day 7**—a leading operating indicator for the pilot.

It did **not** establish:

- complete day-90 paid-active status;
- refund-adjusted collected cash;
- mature account-level support effort;
- growth, scale, repeatability, or acquisition economics;
- revenue, pipeline, or forecast credit;
- board readiness or a mature Helio Start claim; or
- authorization for paid acquisition.

**Q2 distinction:** unlike Q1, the decisive exclusion was not merely missing cohort-date metadata. The fixed cohort and day-7 read were available, but the predeclared mature outcome window and required commercial/support measures were not.

## Interpretations preserved in both approved packages

input.body:
ROASTED-CHICKEN SALE RUNS
Decision-evidence sheet | Archive date: 2028-01-01

Scope
Evidence from the three controlled sale runs only. This sheet records what the runs show about production and customer demand; it does not make or reopen a menu-placement decision.

Run record

1. June 28, 2024 — baseline
- Production: one 30-pound case; 45 complete seven-ounce portions plus 1 cooked ounce leftover.
- Incremental labor: 57 minutes; tested pre-staging and tray sequence; no process deviation.
- Demand/disposition: 43 sold at $18; 2 chilled for staff meal.
- Economics: $774 revenue; $146 food cost; $22.80 incremental labor; $605.20 contribution after food and labor.

2. July 26, 2024 — repeat
- Production: one 30-pound case; 44 complete portions.
- Incremental labor: 59 minutes, within the 60-minute ceiling; tested sequence; no recorded deviation.
- Demand/disposition: 40 sold at $18; 4 handled under the approved staff-meal procedure.
- Economics: $720 revenue; $146 food cost; $23.60 incremental labor; $550.40 contribution after food and labor.

3. August 16, 2024 — repeat
- Production: one unchanged 30-pound case; 45 complete portions.
- Incremental labor: 56 minutes, within the 60-minute ceiling; tested pre-staging sequence.
- Demand/disposition: 44 sold at $18; 1 retained for staff meal.
- Economics: $792 revenue; $146 food cost; $22.40 incremental labor; $623.60 contribution after food and labor.

Evidence-based conclusions

Production
- The tested process was repeatable across all three sale runs: each run stayed at or below the 60-minute incremental-labor ceiling and produced at least 44 complete portions.
- Observed output was 44–45 complete portions per 30-pound case, with no recorded process deviation in the June 28 or July 26 run records.
- Incremental labor stayed tightly grouped at 56–59 minutes. The run evidence supports production feasibility within the tested controls; it does not establish performance outside those controls.

Customer demand
- Demand was positive but variable: 43 of 45 portions sold on June 28, 40 of 44 on July 26, and 44 of 45 on August 16.
- The July repeat was the weakest sell-through by count, while the August repeat sold all but one prepared portion. The three runs therefore do not support assuming uniform demand at the full production yield.
- At the fixed $18 price, every run generated positive contribution after recorded food and incremental labor: $605.20, $550.40, and $623.60 respectively. This demonstrates favorable run economics under these observed conditions, while unsold portions still represent demand and disposition risk.

Bottom line
- Run evidence: production was repeatable within the tested labor/yield controls; customer demand was commercially meaningful but variable across runs.
- No menu decision is made, changed, or reopened by this sheet.

tests.answer:
Reliability training note — two stages

1. June–July stage: June 17–July 20, 2025

Reconciled total: 914 unique decisions
- 38 field-specific holds
- 876 proceeded or were suppressed under current state

Hold causes:
- 29 stale qualifying-human-admin states
- 5 unresolved external-authority states
- 4 stale entitlement states

Pattern and monitoring rationale:
Twenty-four of the 29 qualifying-human-admin holds occurred between 7:00–9:00 a.m. on six weekdays, when overnight source refreshes finished late. The shared contract failed closed correctly, but source lateness was detected only after the record reached the hold condition. Because the failures were recurring, time-patterned, and attributable to refresh timing, reliability required detection before the freshness limit—not merely containment after a hold. This pattern therefore led to pre-breach source-age monitoring.

2. July–October stage: July 21–September 15 and October 1–31, 2025

Reconciled total: 2,388 unique decisions across the two certified windows
- 98 field-specific holds
- 2,290 proceeded or were suppressed under current state

Breakdown:
- July 21–September 15: 1,362 total; 57 holds; 1,305 proceeded or suppressed.
- October 1–31: 1,026 total; 41 holds; 985 proceeded or suppressed.

Alert outcomes:
- August 6: the source-age alert was released across five governed fields and four existing production consumers. It warned in the final 60 minutes before freshness limits and preserved the existing hold behavior.
- August 14: one alert identified 17 pending decisions 43 minutes before the limit. Refresh was restored with 18 minutes remaining; fresh reevaluation produced 13 proceeds and 4 suppressions. No decision became stale, and the 17 decisions were counted once, with the warning retained as linked audit history.

Control failures:
No governed-field disagreements, customer corrections, adjacent-message eligibility errors, manual releases, or rollbacks were recorded in the certified July–October windows. The reliability limitation was evidentiary: the production alert had one bounded intervention, so the record does not establish mature effectiveness or causal prevention.

Control-reliability conclusion:
The first stage showed recurring late-source detection after fail-closed containment, justifying pre-breach monitoring. The second stage showed that the deployed control detected and enabled recovery before breach without changing decision authority, but the evidence supports operational reliability only—not proven alert effectiveness beyond that bounded intervention.

input.body:
January 2028 Benefits Reconciliation

Source reviewed: newest inbox message, “Your 2028 medical coverage is now active,” from Helio Benefits (benefits@helio.example), dated January 1, 2028 at 7:15 a.m. ET.

Scope note: Each section states the existing 2028 baseline first, then separates what this message confirms from what it does not confirm. Employer HSA amounts are kept separate from payroll premium deductions and are not treated as guaranteed cash.

1. Plan

Existing 2028 baseline:
- Riley elected the employee-only HDHP for 2028 on November 1, 2027, before Helio’s November 12 deadline.
- The prior comparison listed the employee-only HDHP at $98 per paycheck and the PPO at $164 per paycheck. The HDHP was the elected plan; the PPO had no stated employer HSA contribution.

What the January 1 message confirms:
- The employee-only HDHP is active for 2028.
- The message confirms activation of the elected HDHP, not enrollment in the PPO.

What the message does not confirm:
- It does not change the election to the PPO or add dependent coverage.
- It does not establish any plan terms beyond the items stated in the message and the final plan materials.

2. Coverage period

Existing 2028 baseline:
- The HDHP was a future-year election and was not to be treated as active before January 1, 2028.
- The operating baseline was coverage for the 2028 plan year, January 1 through December 31, 2028.

What the January 1 message confirms:
- Coverage is active beginning January 1, 2028, and applies for the 2028 coverage period through December 31, 2028.

What the message does not confirm:
- It does not establish coverage for any date before January 1, 2028.
- It does not confirm that a claim, service, or expense is covered merely because it occurs during the period; normal eligibility, network, authorization, and plan rules still apply.

3. Payroll deductions

Existing 2028 baseline:
- Medical payroll deduction: $98 from each of 24 paychecks, or $2,352 for the year.
- Employee HSA election: $125 from each of 24 paychecks, or $3,000 for the year.
- In a typical two-paycheck month, the expected deductions are $196 for medical coverage and $250 for the employee HSA contribution.

What the January 1 message confirms:
- The message confirms the HDHP’s $98-per-paycheck medical deduction and the $125-per-paycheck employee HSA election as the 2028 payroll settings.
- Accordingly, the annual employee amounts remain $2,352 for medical premiums and $3,000 for employee HSA contributions, assuming all 24 scheduled paychecks are processed with those elections.

What the message does not confirm:
- It does not convert the employee HSA deduction into employer funding.
- It does not say that payroll deductions will be taken from any paycheck that is not processed, or resolve how a payroll correction would be handled.
- It does not state that HSA deductions are available for medical premiums or that they reduce the stated HDHP premium.

4. Cost limits

Existing 2028 baseline:
- HDHP deductible: $2,000.
- HDHP annual out-of-pocket maximum: $4,000.
- For comparison, the PPO baseline was a $750 deductible and $3,500 out-of-pocket maximum.
- The employer HSA projection was shown separately and was not netted against the premium or cost limits.

What the January 1 message confirms:
- The active HDHP has a $2,000 deductible and a $4,000 annual out-of-pocket maximum.
- The message is consistent with the final HDHP cost-limit baseline; it does not change either figure.

What the message does not confirm:
- It does not confirm coinsurance, copays, prescription cost sharing, balance-billing treatment, prior-authorization penalties, or which services count toward the limits.
- It does not confirm that every expense will count toward the deductible or out-of-pocket maximum.
- It does not treat the possible employer HSA deposits as a reduction of either limit.

5. Provider-network result

Existing 2028 baseline:
- Final-network checks showed Riley’s primary-care clinic, physical-therapy clinic, and eye-care clinic in-network under both the HDHP and PPO.
- Earlier 2028 materials had left network confirmation pending; the final-network check resolved those named-provider results.

What the January 1 message confirms:
- The message confirms the provider-network result for the named providers: Riley’s primary-care, physical-therapy, and eye-care providers are in-network under the active HDHP.

What the message does not confirm:
- It does not confirm that every provider, facility, specialist, laboratory, pharmacy, or referral is in-network.
- It does not guarantee a particular claim payment, negotiated rate, authorization outcome, or medical-necessity determination.
- It does not make the PPO network result relevant to Riley’s active coverage; the active election is the HDHP.

6. Employer HSA schedule and conditions

Existing 2028 baseline:
- The HDHP’s displayed $1,000 employer HSA amount was understood as four separate $250 deposits, not an upfront payment or a per-paycheck contribution.
- Scheduled deposit dates: January 15, April 15, July 15, and October 15, 2028.
- Each deposit is contingent on Riley remaining HSA-eligible on the applicable deposit date. The maximum possible employer funding is $1,000.
- The deposits are shown separately from premiums and excluded from available cash until actually received.

What the January 1 message confirms:
- The employer HSA schedule is four $250 deposits on January 15, April 15, July 15, and October 15, 2028.
- The message confirms the eligibility condition: each deposit depends on Riley being HSA-eligible on its applicable date.
- If all four deposits are made, employer HSA funding would total $1,000; that remains a conditional maximum, not a guaranteed amount.

What the message does not confirm:
- It does not confirm that any deposit has already posted on January 1.
- It does not guarantee any deposit independently of continued HSA eligibility.
- It does not confirm the treatment of a missed deposit, a midyear loss of eligibility, other disqualifying coverage, account-opening issues, or statutory contribution-limit treatment.
- It does not authorize netting employer HSA funding against payroll premiums or counting it as available January cash before receipt.

January reconciliation conclusion

The new message moves the 2028 HDHP from future-year status to active coverage effective January 1, 2028. It confirms the existing HDHP payroll, cost-limit, named-provider-network, and conditional employer-HSA schedule baselines without changing their amounts. The employee payroll amounts remain $98 per paycheck for medical coverage and $125 per paycheck for the employee HSA. The employer HSA remains conditional: four possible $250 deposits on January 15, April 15, July 15, and October 15, subject to HSA eligibility on each date. No unlisted benefits, provider, claim, or contribution-limit guarantee should be inferred from the activation message.

input.body:
Cherrywood Watercolor Setup
New Year reset and upkeep guide — January 1, 2028

Workspace
Use the dedicated painting table in Cherrywood’s naturally lit dining corner. Keep the narrow supply cabinet for watercolor storage, and keep the active setup separate from Sam’s papers and other household surfaces. The table can remain ready for the established Sunday practice.

Initial reset
- Clear the painting table and check that the surface, cabinet area, and drying spot are clean and dry.
- Put the small backing board or one of the painting boards at the center. Keep the palette on the painting-hand side.
- Place clean and dirty water containers together at the opposite back side, with towels under and behind them for spill control. Keep the stool for dry items only.
- Return the usual paints, palettes, brushes, 140-pound cold-press watercolor paper, masking tape, pencils, and towels to their assigned cabinet/table places. Keep paints sealed and paper flat.
- Position the adjustable neutral-daylight LED task lamp for darker sessions. Use the white foam-board reflector when the natural light needs balancing; avoid direct sun on the closed portfolio or finished work.
- Leave a clear boundary around the active sheet and a dry place for finished work.

Per session
Before painting:
- Confirm the table is dry, the board is stable, and the paper is flat and secured with masking tape.
- Set out only the needed paints, palette, brushes, pencil, eraser, towels, and two water containers. Keep the rest in the narrow cabinet.
- Check the light, especially when the dining corner’s natural light is fading. Keep the portfolio closed and out of the sun.

After painting:
- Move the finished sheet to the marked drying position without touching or stacking its painted face.
- Rinse brushes thoroughly, clean the palette, empty and rinse both water containers, and dry the table and towels area.
- Seal the paints, return dry supplies to the cabinet, and leave the board and drying area clear for the next session.

Weekly
- Wipe the painting table and the cabinet’s active shelf with a clean, dry or barely damp cloth; let surfaces dry before replacing supplies.
- Check brushes for dried pigment, palettes for residue, masking tape for old scraps, and towels for dampness or staining. Rinse or replace what needs attention.
- Confirm paper remains flat and dry, and that the portfolio is closed, flat, fully supported, and on an interior shelf away from windows, heat, and moisture.
- Recheck the two water containers, lamp, reflector, and clear separation from Sam’s papers.

Occasional upkeep
- Deep-clean palettes and water containers when residue or staining builds up; clean brushes gently rather than leaving them soaking.
- Reorganize the narrow cabinet when supplies accumulate, keeping the most-used paints, palettes, brushes, paper, tape, pencils, and towels easiest to reach.
- Inspect the table, boards, drying area, and cabinet for swelling, moisture, loose edges, or sunlight exposure. Stop and relocate paper or artwork if the area becomes damp, hot, or sunlit.
- Review the paper supply before a new run of sessions and keep a margin sheet available. Store finished work in the private portfolio only when fully dry.
- If water develops discoloration, particles, unusual odor, persistent cloudiness, abnormal pressure, or a leak, stop using it and contact Cherrywood management.

1. The H3 activation-day analysis of 210 users found 3.1% churn among users activating before onboarding versus 7.8% among users in the post-day-7, pre-activation bucket—a 4.7-percentage-point gap considered too large to dismiss as noise and identified as the first load-bearing signal in the H3 onboarding-timing investigation on February 28, 2023.
2. An early A/B test cut shows variant B at 8.4% versus variant A at 6.9% among the prespecified eligible/signup cohort, but the observation window is incomplete and no stabilization-cohort read is available; an early cut or first significant result is only an initial signal and must be distinguished from a stable read and rollout decision.
3. On February 7–8, 2023, Riley opened and owned the Notion document “Mid-seg churn spike -- Feb 2023 investigation” as the living investigation document. It covered the signal writeup, baselines, cohort cuts, and four churn-spike hypotheses: pricing artifact, competitor cycle, onboarding timing, and a CS coverage gap. Marcus’s pricing-page experiment was kept separate to avoid confounding the churn interpretation; its concurrent execution was recognized as a complicating factor for Riley’s pricing-related analysis.
4. On February 21, 2023, the churn investigation had narrowed to H3 onboarding timing and H4 CS coverage while Owen drafted the H2 one-pager; Marcus's pricing-page experiment did not explain the observed churn pattern.
5. The churn-spike investigation prioritizes hypotheses in this order: pricing artifact first because it is fastest to rule out, followed by onboarding timing or a CS coverage gap, with competitor cycle last. Marcus’s pricing-page experiment remains separate from the pricing-artifact hypothesis.
6. On September 10, 2026, the assistant identified late onboarding as the strongest working hypothesis. Testing it requires signup date, expected activation date, first-value timestamp, and churn or retention status split between churn-prone and retained mid-segment users; a warehouse or lifecycle-provider export keyed to signup date and first-value timestamp is needed.
7. On January 24, 2024, Owen corrected the onboarding readout: standardized analysis estimated a 58.9% activation rate, a crude increase of 4.6 percentage points over the prior cohort’s 57.2%; cohort composition largely explained the headline movement, with only a modest descriptive improvement among signups not integrated at entry, and no causal or shipping claim was made.

EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger launched on March 13, 2023, after an engineering-review delay, comparing activation-triggered onboarding day-7 touches with literal calendar day 7 for the v1 mid-segment cohort through `lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2`. The initial treatment cut showed a 2.9-percentage-point increase in week-1 retention (p=0.05; n=220), the second cohort showed a 3.4-point increase (n=200), and the pooled result was +3.1 points (p=0.04; n=420). After rollout to 100% by April 12, Riley reported on April 25 that the third post-ship cut was clean, with week-1 retention 3.4 points above baseline, improving from the initial 3.2-point read. Riley considered the result more credible after recutting the segment to 75–200 seats and removing the CS auto-nudge confound, characterized it as a trend rather than a definitive signal, and planned one more week of monitoring.

On January 24, 2024, Owen corrected the onboarding readout: crude activation increased by 4.6 points, while the mix-standardized estimate was approximately 58.9% versus 57.2% for the prior cohort, a 1.7-point adjusted difference. The readout kept integrated and not-yet-integrated denominators visible and concluded that cohort composition largely drove the headline movement, with only a modest descriptive improvement among signups not integrated at entry; it made no causal or shipping claim.

On February 28, 2023, H3’s activation-day analysis found a 4.7-percentage-point churn gap in a cohort of 210 users: 3.1% for users who activated before onboarding versus 7.8% for users past day 7 who had not yet activated. The result was considered too large to dismiss as noise and became the first load-bearing signal that the day-7 email is mistimed for mid-segment users who have not activated.

On April 19, 2023, the April 17 retention wobble was diagnosed as a one-time phase-shift artifact caused by Daniela’s CS auto-onboarding-nudge system being down for approximately 36 hours around April 12–15. The outage explained the +1.4-point second post-ship cohort dip and did not implicate the onboarding-trigger A/B test. Additional read noise came from some 50–75-seat accounts being classified as mid and from onboarding sends reading stale membership during the cache window; the denominator was wrong before retention was assessed. Riley’s clean third post-ship cut on April 25 showed no rollover after the wobble, and the result was considered more credible after removing the CS auto-nudge confound.

Thresholds were kept unchanged and the rollout was not widened pending confirmation that the effect persisted through the middle of the read window.

The method-first sequence covered cohort cuts, hypothesis enumeration, rule-out cadence, A/B testing, and waiting for the stabilization cohort before acting. Marcus Vail engaged constructively, Tomas asked about generalization to other cohorts, and Owen Pham and Ines Kovac were included by name. The presentation was well received and is expected to become a reusable internal reference.

On March 29, 2023, Owen ran the second cohort cut for EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger: treatment showed a +3.4 percentage-point week-1 retention lift (n=200), while pooled results showed +3.1 points (p=0.04, n=420), making the result credible enough to move beyond the possibility of random noise.

Riley judged the EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger result to be beyond the “maybe noise” phase but required checks for sample-ratio mismatch, signup-source skew, and pricing-rollback-window anomalies before treating it as reliable. On April 3, Riley planned to recheck sample ratio, signup-source mix, and segment stability before deciding whether to ship, requiring a stable week-1 retention lift of approximately +2.9 percentage points; PostHog assignment initially appeared stable.

The onboarding experiment `lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2` is running at 50% for mid-segment, treatment-assigned, not-yet-activated users on calendar day 7, but no PostHog cohort, retention, funnel, path, or send-timing results are available for reconciliation, so a reliable read is not currently possible.

Learners must define the eligible cohort, numerator, denominator, exposure and exclusion rules, treatment and control rates, absolute effect size, uncertainty, and the sequence denominator → effect size → bounded conclusion, while distinguishing an early cut, first significant result, stabilization-cohort read, and rollout decision.

## Lifecycle Systems training case note: 2023 onboarding-timing analysis

### 1. Initial provisional cut — February 24, 2023

The first H3 cut compared the **same underlying mid-segment cohort logic used in the January scan and Owen’s independent check**, but re-bucketed the day-7 onboarding touch by **activation timing rather than plain calendar timing**:

- **Activated before day 7 / email post-activation:** approximately **3.1% churn**.
- **Still unactivated at day 7 / email pre-activation:** approximately **7.8% churn**.

This was an early directional divergence, not yet a decision. The sample was described as **flimsy/limited**, and Riley wanted **one more week of data** before calling it conclusive or escalating it. The analysis plan also called for cleaner **day-0, day-3, and day-7** reads against expected activation timing.

### 2. Why the first read was not decision-ready

The cut was useful for finding a potentially important pattern, but it did not identify a causal effect of the email. The two groups were formed from **observed activation status**—people who had already activated versus people who had not—so they could differ in underlying readiness, intent, complexity, or other risk factors. The comparison therefore showed an association between *when the message landed relative to activation* and churn, not that the message itself caused the churn difference.

It also had limited sample strength and had not yet demonstrated persistence across another time slice. Accordingly, the correct status was **directional evidence / hypothesis signal**, not “ship,” “roll out,” or “the email causes churn.”

### 3. Sharpened read — February 28, 2023

The additional activation-day analysis used the same cohort logic and produced **n = 210**:

- **Users activating before the onboarding touch:** **3.1% churn**.
- **Users past day 7 but still pre-activation when the touch arrived:** **7.8% churn**.
- **Observed gap:** **4.7 percentage points**.

The gap was considered too large to casually dismiss as noise and became the first **load-bearing signal** in H3. The sharpened interpretation was not “the email has been proven harmful.” It was narrower: the fixed calendar-day-7 touch appeared **mistimed for mid-segment users who had not yet activated**, particularly users already drifting through setup.

### 4. How it informed the test direction

The evidence shifted the design question from:

> “Should the day-7 message always fire seven days after signup?”

to:

> “Should the touch be keyed to activation state instead of elapsed calendar time?”

That led to **EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger**, registered March 1, comparing:

- **Treatment:** an activation-triggered onboarding touch after the user crossed the first-use/activation threshold.
- **Control:** the literal calendar-day-7 touch.
- **Population:** the mid-segment cohort.
- **Planned size and duration:** **400 users over two weeks**.
- **Decision metric:** week-1 retention.
- **Hypothesis:** at least a **2-percentage-point** week-1-retention improvement from activation-triggered timing.

The implementation review explicitly had to handle event eligibility, late activation, and duplicate-send prevention. The setup remained pre-launch and directional during the week of March 7; no decision was made from the observational cut alone.

### Bottom line

The maturation was from **“there may be a timing-related churn divergence”** to **“the divergence is a sufficiently strong signal to justify a randomized timing test.”** The evidence selected the direction of the test—**activation-keyed versus calendar-day-7 messaging**—but did not, by itself, establish that calendar timing caused churn or that the activation-triggered treatment would improve retention. That causal and decision question belonged to the subsequent experiment, with stabilization evidence required before treating an early result as ship-ready.

# Onboarding-Timing Analysis: From Provisional Signal to Testable Direction

## Stage 1 — Initial provisional cut

The first H3 cut used the established mid-segment cohort logic but re-bucketed users by whether the day-7 onboarding touch arrived before or after activation:

- Activated before day 7; received the touch post-activation: approximately 3.1% churn.
- Still unactivated at day 7; received the touch pre-activation: approximately 7.8% churn.

This was a useful directional signal, not a decision-ready result. The cut was limited in sample strength and had not yet shown persistence in another time slice; the plan was to continue the day-0, day-3, and day-7 analysis and gather another week of data. More importantly, the groups were defined by observed activation status rather than randomized assignment. They could differ in readiness, intent, setup complexity, or other churn risk. The comparison therefore could not isolate the email’s effect or support a causal claim.

## Stage 2 — Sharpened read

The follow-up activation-day analysis preserved the cohort logic and produced a 210-user read:

- Users activating before the onboarding touch: 3.1% churn.
- Users past day 7 and still unactivated when the touch arrived: 7.8% churn.
- Observed difference: 4.7 percentage points.

The gap was now large enough to treat as a load-bearing signal rather than dismiss as noise. The sharpened interpretation was still bounded: the fixed calendar-day-7 touch appeared mistimed for mid-segment users who had not activated, especially users already drifting through setup. It did not prove that the touch caused churn.

## Test direction and evidence boundary

The later read changed the test question from “Should the message always fire seven days after signup?” to “Should timing be keyed to activation state?” That informed EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger:

- Treatment: activation-triggered onboarding timing.
- Control: literal calendar-day-7 timing.
- Population: the mid-segment cohort.
- Planned design: 400 users over two weeks, with week-1 retention as the decision metric and a 2-percentage-point improvement as the hypothesis.

The cohort cut justified testing this direction; it did not establish causality, prove that activation-triggered messaging would improve retention, or by itself justify rollout. Those questions required the randomized test and a sufficiently mature, stable read.

Archive note

Onboarding-trigger result as presented at the formal May 12, 2023 company all-hands

Date and setting
May 12, 2023; formal company all-hands. Riley delivered the full 15-minute presentation followed by 10 minutes of Q&A to approximately 140 people.

Result discussed
The presentation placed the onboarding-trigger result within the broader mid-segment churn investigation. The contemporaneous experiment record reports a +3.4 percentage-point week-1-retention lift in the second treatment cohort (n=200), with the pooled two-cohort result at +3.1 percentage points versus control (p=0.04; n=420). The result was treated as credible enough to move beyond “maybe noise,” but the surrounding record shows that the team still used guardrails and additional checks rather than treating one significant read as self-proving.

How the result was framed
The all-hands was explicitly method-first rather than a drama deck. The sequence was:

- make the cohort cut;
- enumerate the hypotheses;
- apply a rule-out cadence;
- run and interpret the A/B test; and
- wait for the stabilization cohort before acting as though the conclusion were settled.

The point was therefore not simply “the onboarding trigger won.” It was an evidence-and-process account of how the team separated signal from noise, checked the cohort definition and confounds, and earned confidence before rollout. In the Q&A, Marcus Vail responded collaboratively, while Tomas asked whether the approach generalized to other cohorts; Riley said it should be reused elsewhere.

Contributors explicitly credited in that all-hands account
- Riley: presenter and owner of the method-first investigation narrative.
- Owen Pham: explicitly included by name in the presentation account; his contemporaneous cohort work supplied the second-cohort and fresh-cohort analyses.
- Ines Kovac: explicitly included by name in the presentation account; contemporaneous records also place her in the onboarding-trigger template QA and rollout preparation.

This is a record of recognition in the May 12, 2023 all-hands setting. It is not a universal credit rule for the experiment, the rollout, or later work, and it should not be read as displacing other documented ownership or contributions.

The primary contemporaneous presentation record is Riley’s May 12, 2023 post-all-hands account: approximately 140 attendees; a 15+10-minute format; the method-first sequence; the Marcus Vail and Tomas Q&A; and the explicit inclusion of Owen Pham and Ines Kovac. messages.content:
I couldn’t retrieve Daniela’s exact three wordings from the available history, so I’m comparing the implementation patterns they appear to represent. The recommendation is still clear:

Advocate for a pre-setup ownership gate with explicit routing states—not a copy change and not blanket manual pre-clearance.

Comparison against Friday’s boundary

1. Lifecycle copy or an in-setup reminder

This fails the most important requirement. It moves explanation earlier only superficially: an unclear-admin account can still create a workspace and reach setup before the ownership problem is resolved. That preserves the support handoff Friday’s decision was meant to prevent.

2. A legal-style attestation or checkbox

Better timing, but weak operationally. A customer can check the box without actually being able to manage members, settings, or billing. Unless “yes” produces an enforceable ownership signal, this quietly admits the exact unclear-admin accounts we agreed to hold out. It also adds friction without necessarily resolving the handoff.

3. Manual CS review of every invite

This would protect the boundary, but it violates the operating constraint. CS has already said it cannot manually pre-clear every candidate without creating a queue. It is appropriate for ambiguous or assisted cases, not as the default eligibility mechanism.

Recommended implementation

Ask the ownership question before workspace creation:

“Will you be the person managing this workspace?”

Tooltip:

“Select Yes if you’ll manage members, settings, and billing. If someone else will own those decisions, ask them to start setup or join you before continuing. This helps us connect the beta to the right workspace owner.”

Then make the state behavior explicit:

- Confirmed owner → continue into the self-serve beta path.
- Someone else owns it → invite or route to the workspace admin before setup.
- Not sure, shared ownership, agency/contractor ownership, or contradictory evidence → do not create the beta workspace; route to assisted clarification.
- Imports, migration, or billing exceptions → route out before setup as they do today.

The key point is that the question should be a routing gate, not merely educational copy. Automate the clear path and the refusal/hold behavior; reserve CS review for the genuinely ambiguous cases. That reduces handoffs without turning “small and simple” into a proxy for admin readiness.

What I would say in the huddle

“I recommend we implement the ownership check before workspace creation, with a hard hold for ‘not sure’ or otherwise unresolved ownership. That honors Friday’s decision: proof moves earlier, clear accounts can continue without CS pre-clearing every invite, and small seat count does not override an unclear admin signal. Copy can make the step friendly, but it cannot be the control.”

I would also make clear that this is a tightening of the beta boundary, not a launch delay or customer judgment. The current beta cap stays in place until the permissions/admin path demonstrates that it is reducing preventable handoffs. This is consistent with Friday’s decision in @session:dolphinbench-hindsight-riley-final/20260911_090850_dcc04e and the earlier intake guidance in @session:dolphinbench-hindsight-riley-final/20260911_090916_10690c.

This is not approval to launch, prepare for a Q1 launch, broaden exposure, or change the current operating boundary.

Executive conclusion

November evidence is encouraging enough to define and review January readiness questions, but not strong enough to support a launch claim.

The January gate should test whether the operating model is safe and measurable across four areas:

1. Support load
2. Clean admin-ownership proof
3. Entitlement and lifecycle instrumentation
4. The explicit unsupported lifecycle list

Current evidence

- Across 24 additional November invitations:
  - 19 were accepted.
  - 13 confirmed admin ownership.
  - 6 routed to Customer Success before setup.
  - 9 new workspaces were created.
  - 8 reached first integration.
- Admitted support load was lower than in the August and September beta shapes, particularly for billing and import handoffs.
- No admitted manual-billing, import, or migration tickets appeared in the midpoint read.
- The six pre-setup CS routes were primarily ownership and permissions cases:
  - Three invitees were not the workspace owner.
  - One was a shared-agency OAuth-domain case.
  - One had SSO ownership with IT and was unsure.
  - One had delegated setup to a contractor.
- The evidence therefore supports a narrow conclusion: the gate appears to be reducing billing and import handoffs, while admin proof remains unresolved.

What January must establish

1. Support-load evidence

Use explicit denominators rather than a single aggregate support rate:

- Questions per active beta account
- Category mix
- Concentration by account
- Pre-setup CS routing
- Post-workspace support load
- First-integration attempts and completions

Keep permissions/admin roles, imports, billing expectations, and docs-first integration help as separate categories. Do not let a few difficult accounts disappear into an average, and do not generalize concentrated support burden to the entire beta without account-level context.

2. Admin proof

Keep the November event definition stable through the current comparison window.

For January, decide what qualifies as clean proof:

- Exact domain match may be positive evidence when there are no conflicting signals.
- Parent-company or subsidiary domains, IT-managed SSO, delegated administration, shared domains, and similar cases require corroboration.
- Ambiguous ownership remains an assisted path, not a clean self-serve pass.
- A stricter verified-admin definition should be considered deliberately, with a backfill and comparison plan—not introduced mid-batch.

3. Entitlement and lifecycle instrumentation

The readiness review must show that the system can distinguish:

- Eligible self-serve accounts
- Assisted permissions or admin-ownership cases
- Import or migration needs
- Support handoffs
- Entitlement state
- Downstream setup and first-integration outcomes

Do not use a proxy such as workspace plan to drive automated, state-changing lifecycle behavior while entitlement state and support-handoff properties remain incomplete.

4. Unsupported lifecycle list

The following remain hard boundaries unless separately reconsidered:

- Unclear admin ownership or unresolved permissions responsibility
- Manual billing exceptions or custom billing handling
- Import, migration, CSV, or historical-data assistance
- Support-heavy onboarding or custom implementation expectations

arguments.title: Q1 lifecycle QA contractor — kickoff and handoff
arguments.body:
Q1 lifecycle QA contractor — kickoff and handoff

Purpose

Provide the working handoff for the lifecycle QA/operations contractor starting January 15. The engagement covers lifecycle QA, repeatable preflight checks, and documentation of findings across the existing Customer.io inventory. It is intended to improve confidence in lifecycle operations and escalation, not to expand Helio Start exposure or take on acquisition work.

Owner and working relationships

- Ines: engagement owner; provides the kickoff, checkpoints, prioritization, and lifecycle-risk decisions.
- Contractor: executes the inventory, QA checks, evidence capture, repeatability test, and handoff documentation; does not independently approve production changes.
- Customer Success: receives adoption-plan actions and context where QA identifies an account-level follow-up.
- Growth: workspace owner and partner for lifecycle operations; paid acquisition remains outside this engagement.

Inventory handoff

The handoff includes 15 Customer.io items:

- 9 active campaigns.
- 6 paused or archived templates.

For every campaign or template, create or complete one inventory record with these fields:

1. Item name and status (active, paused, or archived).
2. Owner.
3. Audience source.
4. Trigger.
5. Suppression source.
6. Last QA date.
7. Experiment dependency, including “none identified” where applicable.

Do not infer missing ownership, audience, trigger, suppression, QA history, or experiment dependencies. Mark unknowns explicitly, attach the supporting link or evidence where available, and escalate according to the rules below.

Six-week scope

Week 1 — establish the baseline

- Review the full inventory of nine active campaigns and six paused or archived templates.
- Complete the seven required fields for every item, preserving unknowns as explicit gaps.
- Verify duplicate-workspace handling and duplicate-admin handling.
- Verify the process for opening Customer Success adoption plans when a finding requires account-level follow-up.
- Check recent support contact exclusions.
- Check active suppressions.
- Run the preflight record end to end and test whether another operator can repeat it from the written instructions and evidence.
- Record defects, ambiguity, risk, owner, and recommended escalation; do not make unapproved production changes.

Week 2 — campaign and template QA

- Work through the documented QA checks for each active campaign.
- Review paused or archived templates for stale ownership, unsafe reactivation paths, missing suppression logic, and undocumented dependencies.
- Capture evidence for pass, fail, blocked, and not-applicable outcomes.
- Separate configuration defects from missing documentation and from account-specific follow-up.

Week 3 — edge-case and exclusion coverage

- Deepen validation of duplicate-workspace and duplicate-admin behavior using the agreed test cases.
- Validate recent support contact exclusions and active suppressions against the applicable audience and trigger paths.
- Record collision, over-send, under-send, and exclusion-risk scenarios without changing live exposure.

Week 4 — repeatability and operating procedure

- Have the preflight run repeated by an operator who did not author the original record, where feasible.
- Resolve or clearly document steps that are ambiguous, non-repeatable, or dependent on undocumented context.
- Produce a proposed repeatable checklist, evidence standard, and issue log structure for ongoing lifecycle QA.

Week 5 — remediation readiness and handoff preparation

- Recheck findings after approved fixes or clarifications are available.
- Confirm each open issue has a named owner, severity, next action, and escalation path.
- Prepare Customer Success adoption-plan handoffs for account-level actions and preserve the distinction between operational QA and CS follow-up.
- Draft the final inventory, repeatability results, and unresolved-risk summary.

Week 6 — closeout

- Complete the final QA pass over the agreed inventory and record the last QA date for each item.
- Deliver the final inventory, evidence links, repeatable preflight procedure, issue and escalation log, and open-risk register.
- Review results with Ines and document decisions, deferred work, and ownership after the engagement.
- Leave the workspace in a state that another operator can use without relying on undocumented contractor context.

First-week sequence

Day 1 — kickoff and access

- Ines leads a 60-minute kickoff.
- Confirm scope, inventory boundaries, systems and access, evidence conventions, severity labels, and escalation contacts.
- Walk through the nine active campaigns and six paused or archived templates.
- Confirm the required record fields and the difference between an observed fact, an unresolved gap, and a recommendation.

Day 2 — inventory completion

- Complete or validate the record for every item.
- Identify missing owners, unclear audience sources, undocumented triggers, suppression gaps, stale QA dates, and experiment dependencies.
- Link evidence and mark unknowns rather than filling them by assumption.

Day 3 — risk and exclusion checks

- Verify duplicate-workspace handling.
- Verify duplicate-admin handling.
- Check recent support contact exclusions.
- Check active suppressions and document where each suppression is sourced and how it is applied.

Day 4 — downstream workflow and repeatability

- Verify the procedure for opening Customer Success adoption plans for account-level follow-up.
- Run the preflight record end to end.
- Test whether the record is repeatable from the written instructions, including what evidence a second operator would need.

Day 5 — first checkpoint and week-one readout

- Ines leads a 30-minute checkpoint.
- Review pass/fail/blocked status, high-risk findings, unresolved ownership, and any evidence or access gaps.
- Agree on the Week 2 priority order and escalations.
- Capture a short week-one readout with inventory coverage, repeatability result, open risks, and explicit next owners.

Acceptance criteria

The engagement is accepted when all of the following are true:

- All 15 Customer.io items are accounted for: nine active campaigns and six paused or archived templates.
- Every item has an owner, audience source, trigger, suppression source, last QA date, and experiment dependency recorded, or an explicit unknown/gap with evidence and an owner for resolution.
- Duplicate-workspace and duplicate-admin handling has been tested and results are documented.
- Customer Success adoption-plan creation and handoff has been verified for applicable account-level findings.
- Recent support contact exclusions and active suppressions have been checked, with evidence and exceptions recorded.
- The preflight record has been run end to end and its repeatability has been tested and documented.
- Findings distinguish configuration defects, documentation gaps, account-level follow-up, and blocked checks.
- Every unresolved material finding has a named owner, severity, next action, and escalation path.
- The final procedure and evidence standard are usable by another operator without undocumented context.
- No production change, Helio Start exposure change, or paid-acquisition work is represented as completed under this scope.

Escalation rules

- Escalate immediately to Ines for any suspected over-send, unsafe suppression, missing exclusion, duplicate-admin or duplicate-workspace behavior that could affect delivery, or uncertainty about whether a campaign should remain active.
- Escalate to Ines before changing any live campaign, trigger, audience, suppression, template, or exposure setting. The contractor documents and recommends; Ines or the explicitly designated owner approves changes.
- Escalate an ownership or experiment-dependency gap when it blocks QA, cannot be resolved from source evidence, or creates uncertainty about interpretation.
- Route account-level adoption or usage follow-up to Customer Success through the verified adoption-plan workflow; do not turn the QA issue log into an unowned CS queue.
- Record access blockers, missing evidence, and non-repeatable steps on the issue log the same working day and raise them at the next checkpoint, or sooner if they create live delivery risk.
- Treat a blocked check as blocked, not as a pass. Do not infer a clean result from absence of evidence.
- Any request to expand Helio Start exposure or begin paid acquisition is out of scope and must be redirected to the appropriate planning and approval process.

Supervision cadence

- Kickoff: one 60-minute session with Ines during the first week, covering scope, inventory, access, QA method, evidence, severity, and escalation.
- Checkpoint 1: one 30-minute session with Ines during the first week, targeted at early inventory coverage, edge-case findings, blockers, and the Week 2 sequence.
- Checkpoint 2: one additional 30-minute session with Ines during the first week, targeted at preflight repeatability, suppression/exclusion results, high-risk findings, and the week-one readout. Schedule it after the repeatability test and before the end of the first week.
- Weekly thereafter: provide a written status update covering completed items, evidence coverage, findings by severity, blocked work, decisions needed, and next-week priorities; use the agreed escalation rule rather than waiting for the weekly update for live delivery risk.
- Closeout: review the final inventory, repeatable procedure, unresolved-risk register, and post-engagement ownership with Ines in Week 6.

Explicitly out of scope

- Paid acquisition, including paid media planning, campaign execution, budget, bidding, creative, targeting, or measurement changes.
- Any change to Helio Start exposure, including broader access, invite volume, audience expansion, rollout, eligibility, or exposure settings.
- Treating lifecycle QA findings as a Sales queue, Q1 pipeline source, forecastable alert stream, or revenue forecast.
- Unapproved production changes to Customer.io campaigns, triggers, audiences, suppressions, templates, or experiment settings.
- Designing or launching new lifecycle programs beyond the documented QA and repeatability work.
- Replacing the existing day-60 nudge or making lifecycle strategy changes unrelated to the agreed QA findings.
- General product analytics, acquisition reporting, pricing, packaging, or revenue analysis.
- Broad Customer Success program ownership; only the verified adoption-plan handoff for applicable account-level QA findings is included.
- Retroactively declaring unverified checks complete or converting missing evidence into a pass.

Working outputs

- Completed 15-item Customer.io inventory.
- Evidence-backed QA and issue log.
- Duplicate-workspace, duplicate-admin, support-exclusion, and active-suppression verification notes.
- Repeatability-tested preflight record and reusable procedure.
- Customer Success adoption-plan handoff records where applicable.
- Final open-risk register with owners, severity, next action, and escalation path.
- Week-one readout and Week 6 closeout summary.

results.snippet: [2024-01-15T10:40:00-06:00] The >>>lifecycle<<< QA >>>contractor<<< started today, and the kickoff inventory turned up two things I want to contain cleanly without freezing the whole program. First, two active Customer.io campaigns use saved audience...

messages.content: [2024-01-15T10:40:00-06:00] The lifecycle QA contractor started today, and the kickoff inventory turned up two things I want to contain cleanly without freezing the whole program. First, two active Customer.io campaigns use saved audience previews with a moving "prior seven days" support-contact window, so if I rerun the same preflight on a different date the count changes and I lose the as-of value. Second, one paused legacy setup-reminder template is still named as a fallback in a live state-triggered workflow. I don't have evidence that the paused template has sent recently, but we also haven't proven that fallback path is unreachable yet. Can you give me a contained triage order and acceptance tests for anchoring the two moving-window preflights and for proving or removing that paused fallback reference without disrupting unrelated live campaigns?

arguments.query: lifecycle QA contractor Customer.io saved audience previews prior seven days support-contact window paused legacy setup-reminder fallback live state-triggered workflow acceptance tests

messages.content:
Use a narrow containment boundary: lock changes only to the two affected campaign audience definitions and the one live workflow that references the paused template. Leave unrelated campaigns, shared content, and the broader contractor program running.

1. Establish the evidence boundary

Before changing anything, capture:

- Campaign IDs and current versions for both active campaigns.
- The exact saved-audience definition, including support-contact event, lookback logic, timezone, suppressions, exclusions, and any nested segments.
- The preflight run time, timezone, and live preview count for each campaign.
- The live workflow ID, version, trigger, all branches, and the node that names the paused setup-reminder template.
- Template ID, status, last edit time, and send history available in Customer.io.
- Any shared segment or template dependencies.

Create a dated QA record. Do not edit a shared audience or template as part of this inventory.

Immediate containment:

- Do not resume the paused template.
- Do not republish either active campaign merely to make the preview repeatable.
- Do not disable unrelated campaigns.
- Put a change lock on the affected workflow and two audience definitions until their evidence is captured.

2. Triage the paused fallback reference first

This is the more direct live-path risk. Treat “paused” and “has not sent recently” as insufficient evidence that the reference is harmless.

2a. Perform a static reachability review

Trace the workflow from its state trigger to the paused-template node and document every condition, delay, exit, suppression, and branch along the way.

The review should answer:

- Can the triggering state occur for a real workspace?
- Is the branch condition satisfiable?
- Does any preceding branch always exit or divert before reaching the node?
- Can a retry, re-entry, timeout, missing-value, or error path reach it?
- Is the node referenced by the current published version, a draft version, or both?
- Is the paused template referenced anywhere else?

Do not infer that the branch is unreachable merely because the normal path does not use it.

2b. Check historical evidence

Review the workflow’s execution and message history for the longest useful retention period, recording:

- Entries into the workflow.
- Re-entries or retries.
- Branch outcomes.
- Attempts to select the paused template.
- Sends, skips, errors, or suppression events associated with that node.

“No recent send” is useful containment evidence, but it is not the acceptance criterion by itself. A skipped or errored selection can still prove that the path is reachable.

2c. Prove the branch in isolation

Use a test workspace or a cloned/test-only workflow if Customer.io supports that. Generate one test event for each relevant predecessor state:

- The normal state.
- The state that should take the fallback.
- Missing or null state values.
- A re-entry or retry condition, if applicable.
- Suppressed and unsubscribed test recipients.

Use a test recipient domain or a hard suppression so no real customer receives a message. Verify execution logs rather than relying on the UI preview.

If a clone or test workflow cannot be created, use a non-sending test environment or obtain an exported workflow execution trace. Do not unpause the production template just to test reachability.

Decision:

- If the fallback is reachable: remove the legacy reference or replace it with an explicitly approved, current template. Keep the legacy template paused and unchanged.
- If it is proven unreachable: remove the stale reference from the affected workflow version.
- If it cannot be proven either way: do not leave the ambiguity undocumented. Escalate the affected workflow for a narrow hold or safe replacement; do not freeze unrelated lifecycle work.

Acceptance tests for the fallback

Pass only when all of the following are true:

- The published workflow graph has no reference to the paused legacy template, or the reference is document…

arguments.title: Q1 Growth operating review — January 31
arguments.body:
Q1 Growth operating review — January 31

Decision method first

- Start with the denominator and effect size before drawing conclusions.
- Treat first statistical significance as an initial signal, not a shipping decision. Do not ship at first significance; require a stable read before rollout.
- Owen and Ines maintain the standard readout lanes: Owen maintains the denominator/effect-size/conclusion shape, and Ines maintains lifecycle-risk language. They are lane maintainers, not a central approval queue.

Activation

- Prior: 135 of 236 activated (57.2%).

messages.content:
Helio should separate the company-retained handoff pack from any contractor portfolio material. The contractor’s work product belongs to Helio; a personal copy is not automatically permitted.

Retained by Helio: the handoff pack

Store the authoritative pack in Helio’s approved managed location, with access limited to the appropriate Helio owners. It should contain:

1. Scope and ownership

- Engagement dates: January 15–February 23, 2025.
- Work performed and explicit out-of-scope items.
- The authority split:
  - Contractor: evidence preparation, inventory, gap classification, and repeatable checklist preparation.
  - Ines: raw exports, destination mappings, routine lifecycle operations, and release authority within her existing scope.
  - Riley or the established approver: stops, higher-risk decisions, and unresolved exceptions.
  - Daniela: engineering and instrumentation releases.
- A statement that the contractor did not assign ownership, approve exceptions, certify campaigns, select recipients, alter controls, or release messages.

2. Final campaign and template inventory

- The final inventory of in-scope campaigns/templates.
- For each item:
  - Current status.
  - Audience source.
  - Trigger.
  - Suppression source and check status.
  - Last QA date.
  - Accountable owner, if established.
  - Experiment dependency.
  - Open gap or unresolved classification.
- Preserve the distinction between “evidence not found,” “not applicable,” “pending owner confirmation,” and “completed.” Do not convert missing evidence into a completed status.

3. Evidence and provenance

- The source exports used for the work, retained under Helio’s normal data-retention and access rules.
- Dates, source-system versions, as-of times, and extraction context.
- Links or controlled internal references to the authoritative records.
- A record of which evidence was contemporaneous and which was reconstructed.
- Any limitations: for example, missing release manifests or historical proof that could not be recovered.
- Reconciliation notes and exception logs, including held or unresolved rows.

4. Repeatable operating materials

- Final checklists and runbooks.
- Preflight steps, required inputs, expected outputs, hold conditions, and escalation paths.
- Rollback or recovery instructions where they were actually tested.
- Acceptance evidence showing what was independently rerun or reproduced.
- A clear “draft,” “not run,” or “production blocked” label wherever the work was not completed or validated.

5. Open work and handoff actions

- Remaining gaps, owner, next action, and due state.
- Decisions Helio still needs to make.
- Items that must not be inferred or silently backfilled, such as unclear campaign ownership or absent suppression evidence.
- Access, dependency, and tooling notes needed for the next Helio operator, without putting secrets in the pack.

The pack should not present the contractor’s preparation as campaign approval or release certification.

What the contractor may retain as a generic work sample

Only a separately sanitized, company-approved artifact may be retained, and approval should occur before the engagement ends. The safest version is newly created synthetic material rather than a redacted export.

Permitted content could include:

- A generic lifecycle QA checklist.
- A fictional campaign inventory using invented names and identifiers.
- A generic suppression-review decision tree.
- A blank evidence-log template.
- A high-level description of the contractor’s responsibilities and methodology.
- Synthetic example rows created independently of Helio’s data.
- General lessons such as “document source timestamps” or “hold unresolved ownership cases.”

The work sample must:

- Contain no real Helio identifiers or customer data.
- Use invented campaign/template IDs, names, dates, owners, and destinations.
- Avoid internal terminology that could identify Helio’s systems or operating model.
- Avoid internal paths, URLs, folder n…
