messages.content: [2024-02-02T08:12:00-06:00] Finance needs my final answer by 4:00 today on the last $820 still uncommitted in the Q1 Growth envelope. Ines can use six additional contractor hours at $135 an hour, so $810 total, to get operator-ready runbooks written for the two highest-risk lifecycle campaigns before the engagement ends. The scope is supposed to stay tight: a reproducible audience query, suppression and duplicate-admin checks, copy-risk boundaries, release criteria, and rollback steps for each campaign. Give me a direct call on whether those bounded deliverables are worth spending almost all of the remainder instead of leaving it unspent, and define acceptance criteria that keep this from turning into an open-ended campaign redesign.

Call: spend the $810 and leave $10 uncommitted.

The bounded runbooks are worth more than the remaining $820 sitting unused because they turn the contractor’s existing lifecycle context into reusable operating controls. They should reduce release risk and make future campaign execution less dependent on Ines or the contractor. This is a good use of the remainder only if Finance approves it as a fixed, six-hour deliverable—not as additional campaign strategy or execution capacity.

Approve:

- Six contractor hours total at $135/hour
- $810 NTE
- Two highest-risk lifecycle campaigns
- Approximately three hours per campaign
- No use of the funds for paid acquisition, campaign expansion, new instrumentation, or redesign
- $10 remains uncommitted

Acceptance criteria

For each campaign, deliver one versioned, operator-ready runbook containing:

1. Audience query
   - Reproducible query or query specification
   - Named source tables/fields and required parameters
   - Explicit inclusion and exclusion logic
   - Expected output fields and a basic validation check

2. Suppression and duplicate-admin checks
   - Suppression list/source identified
   - Duplicate-admin handling defined
   - Permission, role, and ownership edge cases called out
   - A documented pre-release check with pass/fail evidence or sample validation

3. Copy-risk boundaries
   - Approved message purpose and audience
   - Explicit claims or promises the operator must not introduce
   - Escalation path for ambiguous billing, eligibility, permissions, or lifecycle language
   - No new copy strategy beyond documenting the existing boundaries

4. Release criteria
   - Required preflight checks
   - Named owner for approval
   - Conditions that must be true before release
   - Basic post-release monitoring checks
   - Clear stop conditions for an unsafe or invalid audience/message

5. Rollback steps
   - Exact disable, suppression, or audience-removal action
   - Owner authorized to initiate rollback
   - Verification that the campaign has stopped
   - Required follow-up record or notification

Definition of done

A runbook is accepted only when:

- Another trained operator can follow it without asking the contractor to interpret missing steps.
- The audience query and checks are reproducible from the documented inputs.
- At least one dry run, sample validation, or equivalent review confirms the suppression and duplicate-admin logic.
- Release and rollback owners are named.
- The runbook distinguishes required controls from optional improvements.
- Ines confirms that it is usable as an operating artifact, not merely a set of notes.

Scope guardrails

The contractor may clarify existing logic, but may not:

- Redesign campaign objectives, segmentation, or lifecycle strategy
- Rewrite campaigns or create new messaging variants
- Add instrumentation or dashboards
- Run a live launch or optimize performance
- Expand the campaign list beyond the two named campaigns
- Produce recommendations requiring another project
- Spend more than six hours without a separate approval

Suggested Finance wording:

“Approve $810 NTE for six additional contractor hours at $135/hour to produce two fixed-scope, operator-ready lifecycle campaign runbooks. Each runbook will document the reproducible audience query, suppression and duplicate-admin checks, copy-risk boundaries, release criteria, and rollback procedure. The work excludes campaign redesign, new instrumentation, live execution, and optimization. Acceptance is based on reproducibility and operator usability; any additional work requires separate approval. $10 of the Q1 Growth envelope will remain uncommitted.”

arguments.title: Q1 lifecycle QA contractor — kickoff and handoff
arguments.body:
Q1 lifecycle QA contractor — kickoff and handoff

Purpose

Provide the working handoff for the lifecycle QA/operations contractor starting January 15. The engagement covers lifecycle QA, repeatable preflight checks, and documentation of findings across the existing Customer.io inventory. It is intended to improve confidence in lifecycle operations and escalation, not to expand Helio Start exposure or take on acquisition work.

Owner and working relationships

- Ines: engagement owner; provides the kickoff, checkpoints, prioritization, and lifecycle-risk decisions.
- Contractor: executes the inventory, QA checks, evidence capture, repeatability test, and handoff documentation; does not independently approve production changes.
- Customer Success: receives adoption-plan actions and context where QA identifies an account-level follow-up.
- Growth: workspace owner and partner for lifecycle operations; paid acquisition remains outside this engagement.

Inventory handoff

The handoff includes 15 Customer.io items:

- 9 active campaigns.
- 6 paused or archived templates.

For every campaign or template, create or complete one inventory record with these fields:

1. Item name and status (active, paused, or archived).
2. Owner.
3. Audience source.
4. Trigger.
5. Suppression source.
6. Last QA date.
7. Experiment dependency, including “none identified” where applicable.

Do not infer missing ownership, audience, trigger, suppression, QA history, or experiment dependencies. Mark unknowns explicitly, attach the supporting link or evidence where available, and escalate according to the rules below.

Six-week scope

Week 1 — establish the baseline

- Review the full inventory of nine active campaigns and six paused or archived templates.
- Complete the seven required fields for every item, preserving unknowns as explicit gaps.
- Verify duplicate-workspace handling and duplicate-admin handling.
- Verify the process for opening Customer Success adoption plans when a finding requires account-level follow-up.
- Check recent support contact exclusions.
- Check active suppressions.
- Run the preflight record end to end and test whether another operator can repeat it from the written instructions and evidence.
- Record defects, ambiguity, risk, owner, and recommended escalation; do not make unapproved production changes.

Week 2 — campaign and template QA

- Work through the documented QA checks for each active campaign.
- Review paused or archived templates for stale ownership, unsafe reactivation paths, missing suppression logic, and undocumented dependencies.
- Capture evidence for pass, fail, blocked, and not-applicable outcomes.
- Separate configuration defects from missing documentation and from account-specific follow-up.

Week 3 — edge-case and exclusion coverage

- Deepen validation of duplicate-workspace and duplicate-admin behavior using the agreed test cases.
- Validate recent support contact exclusions and active suppressions against the applicable audience and trigger paths.
- Record collision, over-send, under-send, and exclusion-risk scenarios without changing live exposure.

Week 4 — repeatability and operating procedure

- Have the preflight run repeated by an operator who did not author the original record, where feasible.
- Resolve or clearly document steps that are ambiguous, non-repeatable, or dependent on undocumented context.
- Produce a proposed repeatable checklist, evidence standard, and issue log structure for ongoing lifecycle QA.

Week 5 — remediation readiness and handoff preparation

- Recheck findings after approved fixes or clarifications are available.
- Confirm each open issue has a named owner, severity, next action, and escalation path.
- Prepare Customer Success adoption-plan handoffs for account-level actions and preserve the distinction between operational QA and CS follow-up.
- Draft the final inventory, repeatability results, and unresolved-risk summary.

Week 6 — closeout

- Complete the final QA pass over the agreed inventory and record the last QA date for each item.
- Deliver the final inventory, evidence links, repeatable preflight procedure, issue and escalation log, and open-risk register.
- Review results with Ines and document decisions, deferred work, and ownership after the engagement.
- Leave the workspace in a state that another operator can use without relying on undocumented contractor context.

First-week sequence

Day 1 — kickoff and access

- Ines leads a 60-minute kickoff.
- Confirm scope, inventory boundaries, systems and access, evidence conventions, severity labels, and escalation contacts.
- Walk through the nine active campaigns and six paused or archived templates.
- Confirm the required record fields and the difference between an observed fact, an unresolved gap, and a recommendation.

Day 2 — inventory completion

- Complete or validate the record for every item.
- Identify missing owners, unclear audience sources, undocumented triggers, suppression gaps, stale QA dates, and experiment dependencies.
- Link evidence and mark unknowns rather than filling them by assumption.

Day 3 — risk and exclusion checks

- Verify duplicate-workspace handling.
- Verify duplicate-admin handling.
- Check recent support contact exclusions.
- Check active suppressions and document where each suppression is sourced and how it is applied.

Day 4 — downstream workflow and repeatability

- Verify the procedure for opening Customer Success adoption plans for account-level follow-up.
- Run the preflight record end to end.
- Test whether the record is repeatable from the written instructions, including what evidence a second operator would need.

Day 5 — first checkpoint and week-one readout

- Ines leads a 30-minute checkpoint.
- Review pass/fail/blocked status, high-risk findings, unresolved ownership, and any evidence or access gaps.
- Agree on the Week 2 priority order and escalations.
- Capture a short week-one readout with inventory coverage, repeatability result, open risks, and explicit next owners.

Acceptance criteria

The engagement is accepted when all of the following are true:

- All 15 Customer.io items are accounted for: nine active campaigns and six paused or archived templates.
- Every item has an owner, audience source, trigger, suppression source, last QA date, and experiment dependency recorded, or an explicit unknown/gap with evidence and an owner for resolution.
- Duplicate-workspace and duplicate-admin handling has been tested and results are documented.
- Customer Success adoption-plan creation and handoff has been verified for applicable account-level findings.
- Recent support contact exclusions and active suppressions have been checked, with evidence and exceptions recorded.
- The preflight record has been run end to end and its repeatability has been tested and documented.
- Findings distinguish configuration defects, documentation gaps, account-level follow-up, and blocked checks.
- Every unresolved material finding has a named owner, severity, next action, and escalation path.
- The final procedure and evidence standard are usable by another operator without undocumented context.
- No production change, Helio Start exposure change, or paid-acquisition work is represented as completed under this scope.

Escalation rules

- Escalate immediately to Ines for any suspected over-send, unsafe suppression, missing exclusion, duplicate-admin or duplicate-workspace behavior that could affect delivery, or uncertainty about whether a campaign should remain active.
- Escalate to Ines before changing any live campaign, trigger, audience, suppression, template, or exposure setting. The contractor documents and recommends; Ines or the explicitly designated owner approves changes.
- Escalate an ownership or experiment-dependency gap when it blocks QA, cannot be resolved from source evidence, or creates uncertainty about interpretation.
- Route account-level adoption or usage follow-up to Customer Success through the verified adoption-plan workflow; do not turn the QA issue log into an unowned CS queue.
- Record access blockers, missing evidence, and non-repeatable steps on the issue log the same working day and raise them at the next checkpoint, or sooner if they create live delivery risk.
- Treat a blocked check as blocked, not as a pass. Do not infer a clean result from absence of evidence.
- Any request to expand Helio Start exposure or begin paid acquisition is out of scope and must be redirected to the appropriate planning and approval process.

Supervision cadence

- Kickoff: one 60-minute session with Ines during the first week, covering scope, inventory, access, QA method, evidence, severity, and escalation.
- Checkpoint 1: one 30-minute session with Ines during the first week, targeted at early inventory coverage, edge-case findings, blockers, and the Week 2 sequence.
- Checkpoint 2: one additional 30-minute session with Ines during the first week, targeted at preflight repeatability, suppression/exclusion results, high-risk findings, and the week-one readout. Schedule it after the repeatability test and before the end of the first week.
- Weekly thereafter: provide a written status update covering completed items, evidence coverage, findings by severity, blocked work, decisions needed, and next-week priorities; use the agreed escalation rule rather than waiting for the weekly update for live delivery risk.
- Closeout: review the final inventory, repeatable procedure, unresolved-risk register, and post-engagement ownership with Ines in Week 6.

Explicitly out of scope

- Paid acquisition, including paid media planning, campaign execution, budget, bidding, creative, targeting, or measurement changes.
- Any change to Helio Start exposure, including broader access, invite volume, audience expansion, rollout, eligibility, or exposure settings.
- Treating lifecycle QA findings as a Sales queue, Q1 pipeline source, forecastable alert stream, or revenue forecast.
- Unapproved production changes to Customer.io campaigns, triggers, audiences, suppressions, templates, or experiment settings.
- Designing or launching new lifecycle programs beyond the documented QA and repeatability work.
- Replacing the existing day-60 nudge or making lifecycle strategy changes unrelated to the agreed QA findings.
- General product analytics, acquisition reporting, pricing, packaging, or revenue analysis.
- Broad Customer Success program ownership; only the verified adoption-plan handoff for applicable account-level QA findings is included.
- Retroactively declaring unverified checks complete or converting missing evidence into a pass.

Working outputs

- Completed 15-item Customer.io inventory.
- Evidence-backed QA and issue log.
- Duplicate-workspace, duplicate-admin, support-exclusion, and active-suppression verification notes.
- Repeatability-tested preflight record and reusable procedure.
- Customer Success adoption-plan handoff records where applicable.
- Final open-risk register with owners, severity, next action, and escalation path.
- Week-one readout and Week 6 closeout summary.

- Record access blockers, missing evidence, and non-repeatable steps on the issue log the same working day and raise them at the next checkpoint, or sooner if they create live delivery risk.
- Treat a blocked check as blocked, not as a pass. Do not infer a clean result from absence of evidence.
- Any request to expand Helio Start exposure or begin paid acquisition is out of scope and must be redirected to the appropriate planning and approval process.

Supervision cadence

- Kickoff: one 60-minute session with Ines during the first week, covering scope, inventory, access, QA method, evidence, severity, and escalation.
- Checkpoint 1: one 30-minute session with Ines during the first week, targeted at early inventory coverage, edge-case findings, blockers, and the Week 2 sequence.
- Checkpoint 2: one additional 30-minute session with Ines during the first week, targeted at preflight repeatability, suppression/exclusion results, high-risk findings, and the week-one readout. Schedule it after the repeatability test and before the end of the first week.
- Weekly thereafter: provide a written status update covering completed items, evidence coverage, findings by severity, blocked work, decisions needed, and next-week priorities; use the agreed escalation rule rather than waiting for the weekly update for live delivery risk.
- Closeout: review the final inventory, repeatable procedure, unresolved-risk register, and post-engagement ownership with Ines in Week 6.

Explicitly out of scope

- Paid acquisition, including paid media planning, campaign execution, budget, bidding, creative, targeting, or measurement changes.
- Any change to Helio Start exposure, including broader access, invite volume, audience expansion, rollout, eligibility, or exposure settings.
- Treating lifecycle QA findings as a Sales queue, Q1 pipeline source, forecastable alert stream, or revenue forecast.
- Unapproved production changes to Customer.io campaigns, triggers, audiences, suppressions, templates, or experiment settings.
- Designing or launching new lifecycle programs beyond the documented QA and repeatability work.
- Replacing the existing day-60 nudge or making lifecycle strategy changes unrelated to the agreed QA findings.
- General product analytics, acquisition reporting, pricing, packaging, or revenue analysis.
- Broad Customer Success program ownership; only the verified adoption-plan handoff for applicable account-level QA findings is included.
- Retroactively declaring unverified checks complete or converting missing evidence into a pass.

Working outputs

- Completed 15-item Customer.io inventory.
- Evidence-backed QA and issue log.
- Duplicate-workspace, duplicate-admin, support-exclusion, and active-suppression verification notes.
- Repeatability-tested preflight record and reusable procedure.
- Customer Success adoption-plan handoff records where applicable.
- Final open-risk register with owners, severity, next action, and escalation path.
- Week-one readout and Week 6 closeout summary.

arguments.hypothesis: The capped, nonpublic Helio Start cohort may be ready for a controlled-readiness decision on activation, support load, intake routing, exclusions, and operating capacity, but the current evidence does not authorize any public-product, acquisition, pricing, launch, pipeline, or revenue conclusion.

arguments.timeline: Owner inputs received after the February 23, 2024 noon Central cutoff; preread for the February 26 controlled-readiness meeting. Owen's latest quantitative panel is dated February 21, 2024.
arguments.body:
Helio Start readiness cohort — February 26 preread

Purpose and decision boundary

This preread consolidates the four late owner inputs for Monday's controlled-readiness decision. The decision is limited to whether the capped, nonpublic Helio Start operating path is sufficiently understood and controlled across activation, support load, intake routing, exclusions, and operating capacity.

This is not a launch conclusion. Nothing here implies GA, pricing-page exposure, paid acquisition, launch language, forecastable pipeline, or revenue attribution. It does not authorize widening the cohort or changing its public posture.

Evidence map and ownership

- Owen: readiness dashboard and quantitative outcome panel.
- Daniela: instrumentation and data-quality evidence.
- Ines: lifecycle and risk review.
- Customer Success: support load, customer cases, and readiness context.

Quantitative evidence

The panels below answer different questions. Denominators must not be pooled or substituted for one another.

1. Owen's latest mature outcome panel — February 21

- Total invited accepted-self-serve workspace exposure: 107.
- Mature workspaces with a completed seven-day observation window: 92.
- Still-immature workspaces: 15. These remain visible within the 107 exposure count, are not failures, and are excluded from readiness outcome conclusions.
- Activated: 61 of 92 mature workspaces.
- Mature workspaces with at least one customer-initiated support contact: 18 of 92.
- Customer-initiated support contacts: 27 total across the mature panel.
- Concentration: one workspace accounted for five contacts.

Read this panel as mature-workspace activation and support incidence plus contact concentration. The 15 immature workspaces are not folded into the outcome denominator.

2. Corrected mature accepted-self-serve slice

This is a separate corrected slice and must not be blended with Owen's February 21 panel.

- Mature accepted-self-serve denominator: 55, corrected down from 58 in the earlier slice.
- Activated: 37 of 55.
- Self-serve workspaces with customer contact: 10 of 55.
- Self-serve customer-initiated contacts: 14.
- Assisted-routed exclusions: 3 workspaces and 3 contacts, retained in a separate assisted-routing panel and excluded from self-serve outcomes.

The three assisted-routed workspaces count once each in the broader 120-application intake cohort, but not in accepted-self-serve activation or support-outcome denominators. This slice is for denominator hygiene and routing history, not a replacement for the February 21 panel.

3. January readiness intake panel

This panel uses 30 held applications. It is not a 52-item denominator and must remain separate from post-acceptance outcomes.

- Exact-domain automatic passes: 18 of 30 held applications.
- Corroborated parent-company or IT-managed passes: 9 of 30.
- Agency identities routed to Customer Success: 3 of 30.

4. January readiness post-acceptance panel

This panel uses 22 accepted Q4 workspaces.

- Day-7 activated: 14 of 22 Q4 workspaces.
- Workspaces with a support contact: 5 of 22.

The 30 held-application intake panel and the 22-workspace outcome panel describe different stages and are not combined.

5. Q4 closeout context

- Accepted invitees: 50.
- Confirmed admin ownership: 34 of 50 accepted invitees.
- Routed to Customer Success before setup: 16 of 50 accepted invitees.
- Workspaces created: 22.
- First integrations: 19 of 22 workspaces created.

These figures preserve the distinction between invite acceptance, admin ownership, pre-setup routing, workspace creation, and first integration. Inherited or assisted admin ownership remains included in total first integrations and support load where applicable, but is not clean self-serve setup or ordinary docs-first setup.

Qualitative evidence — six Customer Success comments

The six comments are kept separate from the quantitative panels. They are directional case context, not a prevalence estimate, causal evidence, or a reason to override the mature outcome panel. The available record supports the following conservative paraphrases rather than verbatim quotations:

1. Three comments described an invitee who was not the workspace owner. Code: ownership/admin-routing issue. This is an operating-ownership question, not automatically a product-state defect. Owner: Customer Success, with admin-routing/instrumentation follow-up from Daniela where needed.

2. One comment involved a shared-agency OAuth-domain case. Code: external permissions/ownership dependency. Owner: Customer Success for assisted routing and permission confirmation; Daniela for event/state traceability if the case exposes an instrumentation gap.

3. One comment described uncertainty because SSO ownership sat with IT. Code: external dependency plus expectation/ownership ambiguity. Owner: Customer Success for the supported admin handoff; Ines for lifecycle language that makes the required owner and handoff clear.

4. One comment described setup delegated to a contractor. Code: delegated-admin dependency. Owner: Customer Success for the supported assisted path and explicit administrator confirmation.

5. The six comments did not include manual-billing requests. Code: bounded negative qualitative observation. This does not establish that manual billing is absent from the wider cohort; it only describes these six cases. Owner: Ines for boundary language; Customer Success for routing any future exception.

6. The six comments did not include import or migration requests. Code: bounded negative qualitative observation. This is not a prevalence estimate and does not change the unsupported self-serve boundary. Owner: Customer Success for case classification; Daniela for preserving the route and state in the evidence trail.

Qualitative caveat

These six selected comments illustrate possible ownership, permissions, external-dependency, and expectation issues. They do not estimate how common those issues are, establish causality, or override the mature quantitative panel. Keep ownership/admin cases distinct from product-state issues. Treat follow-up as targeted operating work, not as a broad readiness conclusion.

Decision questions for Monday

1. Are the stage-specific denominators, maturity treatment, and assisted-routing exclusions reconciled well enough for a controlled-readiness decision?
2. Is the mature support load understood at both workspace incidence and contact-volume level, including concentration rather than only an average or case count?
3. Are the admin-ownership and pre-setup routing paths explicit, consistently classified, and operationally owned?
4. Are Daniela's instrumentation and data-quality checks sufficient to trust the state and route distinctions without inferring ownership, entitlement, or support state from proxies?
5. Does Ines's lifecycle and risk review keep the path conservative, non-state-changing, and clear about assisted setup, permissions, imports, and unsupported requests?
6. If the answer is controlled readiness, what remains capped, what operating guardrails remain mandatory, and what evidence would be required before any separate future scope decision?

Bounded synthesis

The current evidence is usable for a controlled-readiness discussion: it provides a mature outcome panel, separate maturity treatment, support incidence and concentration, corrected self-serve denominator hygiene, intake-routing evidence, and six bounded qualitative cases. The evidence does not support combining the panels into one funnel or treating the six comments as prevalence evidence.

The decision should therefore be recorded as one of: keep capped pending specific operating work; continue the controlled path with explicit guardrails; or request another evidence cut. Whichever option is chosen, it remains a controlled-readiness operating decision only.

Explicit non-claims

Do not describe this preread or its decision as GA, generally available, publicly launched, pricing-page exposure, a pricing experiment, paid acquisition, a launch commitment, launch language, forecastable pipeline, revenue attribution, or a forecast. Do not imply that the cohort represents broad demand or that the admin path is solved.

Q1 2024 lifecycle contractor — reconciliation worksheet

As-of: January 1, 2028
Purpose: Reconcile the approved engagement against the restored inbox evidence without treating an approval, cap, or envelope as proof that the amount was fully spent.

1. Executive reconciliation

- Approved Q1 Growth envelope: $24,000.
- Original contractor approval / PO cap: $23,180 not-to-exceed.
- Later approved bounded extension: $810 for six additional hours at $135/hour, leaving $10 uncommitted if fully used.
- Revised approval ceiling after the extension: $23,990.
- Observed paid charges in the restored invoice subjects: $17,500 total ($8,400 + $9,100).
- Observed paid charges are $6,500 below the $24,000 envelope, $5,680 below the original $23,180 NTE, and $6,490 below the revised $23,990 ceiling.
- These differences are comparisons only. They do not establish that the remaining amount was unspent, that the extension was used, or that the engagement was fully reconciled.

2. Approved envelope and finance basis — SUPPORTED

Approval and earlier engagement record:

- Priya finalized a $24,000 discretionary Q1 Growth envelope for the lifecycle QA and operations contractor rather than Helio Start paid acquisition.
- Engagement dates: January 15 through February 23, 2024.
- Original approved cost structure:
  - Professional services: $20,400.
  - Vendor administration fee: $1,530 (7.5%).
  - Reimbursable tooling: up to $1,250, only for documented, approved tooling actually used.
  - Original not-to-exceed total: $23,180.
  - Original envelope amount not committed to the PO: $820.
- Later approved bounded extension:
  - Six additional hours at $135/hour.
  - Extension amount: $810.
  - Fixed purpose: two operator-ready runbooks for the two highest-risk lifecycle campaigns.
  - Runbook content: reproducible audience query; suppression and duplicate-admin checks; copy-risk boundaries; release criteria; rollback steps.
  - Guardrail: no open-ended campaign redesign, new instrumentation, live launch, optimization, or work beyond six hours without separate approval.
  - If fully used, revised NTE: $23,990 and remaining envelope: $10.

3. Engagement dates and reporting owner — SUPPORTED

- Covered engagement window: January 15–February 23, 2024.
- Reporting / accountable owner: Ines.
- Ines supervised kickoff, checkpoints, prioritization, lifecycle-risk decisions, and the closeout review.
- Contractor role was preparation and evidence work: inventory, QA checks, evidence capture, repeatability testing, issue classification, runbooks, and handoff documentation. The contractor did not independently approve production changes or release messages.

4. Permitted work categories — SUPPORTED

Base engagement scope:

- Review and QA of the existing Customer.io inventory: nine active campaigns and six paused or archived templates.
- Record owner, audience source, trigger, suppression source, last QA date, and experiment dependency for each item; mark unknowns explicitly rather than infer them.
- Experiment-setup hygiene and repeatable preflight work.
- Duplicate-workspace and duplicate-admin handling checks.
- Recent support-contact exclusion checks.
- Active suppression checks.
- Evidence-backed QA findings, including pass, fail, blocked, and not-applicable states.
- Repeatability testing of the preflight record and production of a reusable checklist / procedure.
- Account-level Customer Success adoption-plan handoffs where a QA finding requires follow-up; not broad Customer Success program ownership.
- Final inventory, issue and escalation log, open-risk register, evidence links, repeatable preflight procedure, and closeout handoff.

Approved extension scope:

- Two fixed-scope operator-ready runbooks for the two highest-risk lifecycle campaigns, limited to the approved six hours.

Tooling:

- Tooling is permitted only as documented, approved, reimbursable actual expense. No tooling spend is evidenced by the restored invoice subjects.

5. Observed charges — SUPPORTED AS OBSERVED, NOT COMPLETE RECONCILIATION

- Invoice LC-101 — Jan 15–Feb 2 lifecycle QA and preflight work — $8,400 — paid.
- Invoice LC-102 — Feb 3–16 lifecycle operations and suppression checks — $9,100 — paid.

- $8,400 + $9,100 = $17,500.

messages.content:
Ownership points for Ines

- Ines owns the operational lifecycle-risk review:
  - Review the intended audience before each send.
  - Identify affected, excluded, and ambiguous audiences.
  - Assess support, qualitative-review, and handoff risks.
  - Document whether the audience is safe to proceed, needs changes, or should be held.

- Ines can own lifecycle suppression decisions:
  - Define and apply suppression rules within the established lifecycle workflow.
  - Hold or exclude users when eligibility, support, admin ownership, billing, or other risk conditions are unclear.
  - Re-run and document the final audience after suppression changes.
  - Keep unresolved classifications explicit rather than treating them as eligible.

- Her ownership is operational, not engineering:
  - She can decide how lifecycle audiences should be handled based on the available signals.
  - She should not be described as owning the underlying event instrumentation, state model, release metadata, connector-state pipeline, or feature-flag registry.

Dependencies she cannot yet control

- The pre-send check depends on release metadata maintained by Daniela’s engineering team.
  - Ines needs reliable confirmation that the relevant release or rollout state is current.
  - She should not be promised direct access, edit rights, or authority over that metadata unless Daniela’s team establishes it.

- The check also depends on connector-state signals maintained by Daniela’s team.
  - Ines can review and act on the signals, but engineering must maintain their production correctness, freshness, schema, and delivery.
  - A stale, missing, delayed, or contradictory connector state should be treated as a dependency or hold condition—not something Ines is expected to repair herself.

- Before discussing a handoff for the shipped day-7 lifecycle flag, verify its registry ownership.
  - Confirm who currently owns the flag in the feature-flag registry.
  - Confirm who can change targeting, rollout, or state.
  - Confirm who is responsible for metadata, monitoring, and rollback.
  - Only then discuss whether operational ownership should move to Ines or remain with Daniela’s team.

Suggested framing

“Ines can own the lifecycle audience review and the decision to suppress, hold, or proceed based on the approved signals. The pre-send check is shared operationally but depends on engineering-controlled release metadata and connector-state data. We should not promise Ines access or authority over those systems until Daniela’s team confirms it. Before we discuss handing off the shipped day-7 flag, we need to verify who owns it in the registry and what permissions and rollback responsibilities that ownership includes.”

Boundary to make explicit

- Ines owns the lifecycle decision and evidence.
- Daniela’s team owns the underlying engineering signals and release infrastructure until a formal ownership change is confirmed.
- No handoff should be implied merely because Ines reviews or acts on the resulting audience.

arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2026 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2026 year-end self-review working draft

1. Evidence-grounded contributions and claim discipline

In 2026, I focused on making operating evidence useful without letting it outrun what the sources could support. For Q1, I kept Expansion Assist within its approved descriptive boundary: 14 actual exposures had complete 45-day windows, with five help-or-options requests and three observed expansions. Because there was no randomized control, this was not evidence of causal lift, pipeline or revenue impact, or forecast credit. I preserved the elapsed-time counting rules and kept later commercial outcomes separate from the approved 45-day read.

For Q2, I kept Helio Start’s paid evidence separate from acquisition, scale, pipeline, and forecast language. The fixed 50-workspace cohort closed with 37 paid-active, six canceled, four past due, and three on billing hold. It produced $60,480 in gross billed cash and $56,230 in refund-adjusted collected cash. The certified 39-of-50 day-7 first-integration result remained a leading operating measure, not mature acquisition evidence; account-level support effort, including a 104-minute 90th-percentile result and seven workspaces above 90 minutes, remained a material limitation. I recommended—and Priya accepted—the decision not to grant a second Helio Start paid batch. Paid traffic remains off, and the cohort receives no pipeline or forecast treatment.

I also helped release the organic Helio Start authority-checklist path. The release was intentionally non-state-changing: eligibility, routing, suppression behavior, and governed state meanings remained unchanged. The checklist appeared only for admitted workspaces with current, verified external authority when the selected connector required an owner-level permission or network-allowlist action. The initial descriptive check covered 44 organic admissions; 13 had verified external authority and received connector-specific checklists, 10 completed the first setup action without support, and three requested ordinary assistance. External-system authority means readiness for the connector-specific owner action, not permission for automated outreach. Suppressed, held, and proceed states retained their existing meanings: active Customer Success adoption or renewal work suppresses action; stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state creates a field-specific hold pending fresh verification and reevaluation; proceed is limited to the evaluated decision and does not grant blanket contact permission. This early, nonrandomized result does not establish activation or support-effort improvement.

2. Leadership through delegation

I moved Owen’s monthly-preparation transition toward a more independent and auditable operating lane while keeping the accountability boundaries explicit. Owen prepares the sanitized monthly campaign snapshot and denominator and evidence-field inputs, documents the operational consequence, and reports routine exceptions using the established workflows. Beginning September 24, he may close routine source-completeness reviews across the four existing evidence lanes—Helio Start, Expansion Assist, pricing-page path quality, and CS auto-nudge controls—only when all required fields are present, definitions are unchanged, named owners have certified their sections, and no cross-surface discrepancy exists.

That is delegated preparation and routine source review, not delegated ownership of consequential judgment. I still participate in routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews, including reviewing exception summaries and testing whether the packet’s evidence supports its stated limits. I retain authority over disputed semantics, evidence boundaries, cross-surface consequences, customer corrections, incident stops, state-changing or exception-heavy matters, board readiness, causal or revenue claims, forecast treatment, and executive language. Missing fields, conflicting definitions, or unresolved discrepancies remain incomplete and escalate to me. Daniela retains engineering release and rollback control, and Ines retains lifecycle-governance limits.

This model has reduced unnecessary line-by-line reconciliation without turning Owen’s preparation work into approval, a board-readiness decision, or authority to make claims. It also makes escalation visible: routine work can move independently when the closure predicates are met, while exceptions remain with the appropriate decision owner.

3. A boundary defended under pressure

A recurring part of my role was preserving the difference between operational readiness, governed state, permission to contact, and permission to make a commercial claim. The organic authority checklist demonstrates that distinction: it helps an eligible, admitted workspace prepare for a connector-specific owner action, but it does not change who is eligible, bypass lifecycle suppression, release a held row, or authorize automated outreach. A held row remains fail-closed until the required state is freshly checked and reevaluated; it is not manually released or sent as catch-up.

I applied the same discipline to the Helio Start paid cohort. Mature descriptive outcomes did not become a second-batch approval, an acquisition claim, a pipeline signal, or forecast input. I kept the paid-pilot decision separate from the organic checklist release and preserved the existing eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, and support-routing rules. The result was a reversible operating improvement with clear meanings, rather than an informal expansion of authority based on encouraging early numbers.

4. Development priorities

First, I will make bounded delegation easier to operate without treating it as complete. In the next review cycle, I will maintain a single handoff and closure rubric for the four evidence lanes, define the required fields and certification checks in the packet template, and record escalation triggers for missing evidence, disputed semantics, cross-surface discrepancies, customer corrections, state changes, and exception-heavy cases. I will use the next comparable monthly packets to check whether Owen can close qualifying routine reviews cleanly while I continue participating in preparation and source-closure review. Success means less avoidable line-by-line reconciliation, no hidden unresolved issues, and clear evidence of where my judgment was still required.

Second, I will sharpen executive decision framing. For each major readout, I will draft the takeaway around the denominator or coverage dates, outcome window, effect size or operating magnitude, maturity status, evidence limits, and decision consequence. I will explicitly separate descriptive or non-significant direction from a ship, growth, revenue, or forecast decision, using the Helio Start and authority-checklist readouts as practice cases. Success means that reviewers can see both what the evidence says and what it does not authorize without relying on implied language.

I remain accountable for final operating claims and escalations, and I continue to contribute to routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews. Owen’s transition changes how routine work is prepared and, under defined conditions, closed; it does not mean that I have left those workflows or transferred my retained claims and exception authority.

arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft

Review context

Priya opened the 2027 self-review window on November 8, 2027, with a first-draft deadline of November 19. This revision is decision-led: it starts with the consequential choices I made, states the evidence and limits behind each choice, and then credits the people who executed their own lanes. It does not treat preparation as approval, operating control as customer outcome, or another person’s execution as my own.

1. Decisions I made and the boundaries I held

My central contribution in 2027 was to make consequential decisions explicit, bounded, reversible, and evidence-aware. I owned the high-stakes decision and final-claim boundary: exception decisions, disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer corrections, incident stops, state-changing or exception-heavy matters, causal and executive-language decisions, revenue and forecast treatment, board readiness, and final operating claims.

I did not own routine source preparation, routine measurement closure, routine lifecycle execution, engineering release execution, or rollback execution. I did not turn a clean operating read into a broader authorization, and I did not claim that a decision I made meant I had performed the underlying owner work.

The year-end evidence framing remained four separate lanes:

1. Helio Start — customer-outcome and operating-control evidence, with organic and paid-source evidence kept separate.
2. Expansion Assist — descriptive evidence for the governed population, retaining its own eligibility definition, exposure denominator, treatment, outcome window, exclusions, and maturity status.
3. Pricing-page path quality and continuity — post-rollout continuity evidence, including sessions, flow starts, admission completion, support-time measures, coverage dates, and metric definitions.
4. CS auto-nudge system controls — system-control evidence covering governed decisions, field-specific holds, freshness and conflict handling, visible outcomes, corrections, disagreements, incidents, monitoring, release, and rollback.

Each lane retained its own denominator, coverage dates, outcome window, exclusions, source-as-of time, reliability evidence, and maturity limits. The incomplete-setup reminder was the fifth shared-state production consumer, not a sixth evidence lane. Its operation stayed within the established boundaries and did not create a reusable audience, broader entitlement, new consumer authority, or transfer of an owner lane.

2. Decision: approve and operate one bounded Helio Start paid-search batch

Decision and my role

I prepared and maintained the bounded Helio Start paid-search proposal and owned its operating boundaries and claim limits. The design was one approved high-intent batch only, closing at the earlier of $8,000 in cumulative paid-source spend or 25 admitted workspaces. Existing eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, freshness, hold, suppression, instrumentation, dedupe, assisted-routing, correction, and incident-stop rules remained unchanged. No additional paid batch was included or implied.

The proposal also preserved explicit stop and pause conditions: stop on an unsupported admission; pause if paid-source attribution could not reconcile from eligibility-flow start through the final route; and, after at least 10 admissions, pause if more than 10% of admitted workspaces exceeded 90 account-level support minutes. The batch did not create a pipeline target or treatment, forecast credit, revenue claim, eligibility change, lifecycle bypass, scale claim, or permission to infer authority from remaining spend or admissions capacity.

Evidence used for the decision

The certified Q2 evidence used to support the constrained decision was descriptive operating evidence: 18 of 25 workspaces were paid-active; refund-adjusted collected cash was $27,860; median account-level support effort was 33 minutes; p90 effort was 116 minutes; and 5 of 25 workspaces exceeded 90 minutes. These inputs supported a bounded operating decision. They were not randomized or causal acquisition evidence and did not establish mature retention, acquisition economics, pipeline contribution, forecast performance, or results for the new cohort.

Explicit credits

Priya approved the budget and the bounded batch. Her approval was the separate budget-and-batch decision; it was not a waiver of the operating boundaries and did not authorize a second batch.

Daniela separately completed the November 1 launch authorization after verifying the launch-day proofs: current attribution endpoints and end-to-end reconciliation; production release, enablement, cap enforcement, audit logging, and rollback controls; and staffed Customer Success owner-and-backup coverage for Monday–Friday, 8:00am–6:00pm Central, with after-hours cases routed to the next service opening. I credit Daniela’s launch authorization and technical/reliability work separately from my proposal and decision-boundary work.

Owen owned the refund-adjusted collected-cash evidence and the measurement/denominator work. Customer Success owned paid-active status, account-level support evidence, staffing, and the staffed handoff. Ines owned lifecycle-control verification and message-state safeguards within her authority. I did not perform or reassign those execution lanes.

Current status and claim limit

The November 1–7 readout recorded 12 paid-source eligibility-flow starts reaching final states: 5 admitted, 4 assisted, and 3 ineligible, with $1,580 spent. Attribution reconciled from eligibility-flow start through each final route; no unsupported applicant was admitted, and no lifecycle hold or suppression was bypassed.

This is live operational work, not mature evidence. The batch remains bounded by the earlier of $8,000 cumulative paid-source spend or 25 admitted workspaces. No mature claim may be made for the new cohort until every admitted workspace has a complete permitted day-90 window. Early counts are operating observations and control evidence, not mature customer outcomes, causal acquisition evidence, revenue evidence, scale evidence, or forecast evidence. The current batch has no pipeline target or treatment, no forecast credit, and no additional-batch authority.

3. Decision: keep the incomplete-setup reminder governed and fail closed

Decision and my role

I maintained the incomplete-setup reminder as a governed evaluated operation rather than converting it into a reusable audience or broader entitlement. The customer-action scope remained unchanged. Every possible display required fresh governed-state evaluation: active Customer Success work suppressed the action; missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state held it; and visible monitoring, source-age alerts, and rollback control remained active.

Explicit credits

Daniela moved the reminder to 100% of otherwise eligible production evaluations and owned the engineering enablement, source/event reliability, monitoring, and rollback path. Ines owned lifecycle governance, message-state controls, suppression and stop behavior, and the authority-checklist escalation within her existing send authority. Owen owned reporting, denominator clarity, source-completeness, and exception classification. I owned the bounded operating decision and the final claim boundary; I did not execute Daniela’s release work, Ines’s lifecycle work, or Owen’s measurement work.

Current status and claim limit

Across November 1–7, the reminder path recorded 12,480 fresh evaluations: 1,615 displayed, 520 were suppressed for current active Customer Success work, 186 were held for missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state, and 10,159 did not display because setup or qualifying-human-administrator conditions were not met. Reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes agreed throughout.

These counts support operating-control and reliability observations only. They do not establish improved activation, reduced support effort, acquisition lift, durable customer value, causal impact, scale readiness, pipeline, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, or executive claims. Proceed, Suppressed, and Held remained mutually exclusive outcomes. Incomplete state was not substituted with stale data or treated as implicit approval.

The reminder is the fifth shared-state consumer, not a sixth. Full release changed no governed-field meaning, created no reusable audience, broadened no authority, and did not authorize a lifecycle bypass. The effective workaround and any underlying service gap remain separate observations; neither should be collapsed into a claim that the institution or service is functioning.

4. Evidence discipline and explicit exclusions

I consistently separated what was observed, what was certified, what was decided, and what remained unavailable. Mature prior-cohort evidence may support a bounded decision without becoming causal evidence. Current paid-batch results remain immature until the permitted outcome windows are complete. Reminder counts are descriptive control evidence. Agreement across reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes supports evaluation-path integrity, not proof of customer improvement.

The exclusions I set and preserved apply across the evidence bank unless stronger evidence and a separately applicable decision support a claim. These materials do not, by themselves, establish:

- causal activation or causal impact;
- reduced support effort or support improvement;
- acquisition lift, acquisition efficiency, or acquisition economics;
- scale readiness or durable customer value;
- revenue impact, pipeline contribution, or pipeline treatment;
- forecast performance or forecast credit;
- board readiness or executive language; or
- mature retention.

Descriptive direction is not a ship, growth, revenue, or forecast decision. Source completeness is not final-claim approval. Operating-control evidence is not proof that the customer or service outcome is mature. No remaining spend or admissions capacity implies permission to continue. No operating result authorizes another batch. No source-complete packet authorizes a claim merely because its fields reconcile. No held state is a clean result, and no mature-window share is automatically final retention.

5. Team development through accurate delegation

I developed the team by delegating bounded work with explicit authority limits and by keeping consequential interpretation with the correct owner.

Owen

Owen owns measurement preparation, definitions, denominator and unit clarity, cross-surface mapping, routine source completeness, the sanitized campaign snapshot, and exception reporting. He closes routine four-lane source review only when required fields are present, definitions are unchanged, named owners have certified their sections, reliability evidence is present, and no cross-surface discrepancy remains. Otherwise he records an explicit incomplete status rather than substituting stale data or silently declaring success.

During the year Owen prepared the sanitized campaign snapshot and per-lane measurement views, maintained denominator and source-completeness discipline, and produced exception syntheses. His October exception synthesis preserved a source-certification delay, kept the work visibly incomplete without stale substitution, and distinguished the issue from missing input, cross-surface discrepancy, disputed semantics, and no exception. His November cycle was correctly classified as no exception. Owen’s work is evidence of independent measurement and exception execution; it is not my execution, and it does not give him readiness, causal-claim, disputed-semantics, narrative, revenue, pipeline, forecast, board-readiness, or executive-language authority.

Ines

Ines owns lifecycle governance, message-state controls, owner-state certification, suppression and stop behavior, and routine non-state-changing lifecycle releases within existing send authority. She kept wording, trigger behavior, audience state, holds, suppressions, and governed-state handling aligned to the approved rules, and she escalated the November authority-checklist case rather than changing the trigger, audience, or release behavior. Her certification is an input to source closure, not a request for my routine approval. Ines’s work is lifecycle-governance and message-state execution; it is not my execution, and it does not transfer final decision or claim authority to either of us.

Daniela

Daniela owns source and event/state reliability, transport reliability, source refresh and freshness monitoring, engineering release, production enablement, monitoring, incident handling, and rollback. Her November 1 authorization was based on the required launch-day proofs and remained scoped to the approved batch. The reminder operation retained fresh evaluation, source-age monitoring, visible holds and suppressions, and rollback readiness. No customer correction, incident stop, failed rollback, or rollback need was recorded in the November 1–7 reminder readout.

These are Daniela’s reliability, release, enablement, monitoring, and rollback contributions. I do not present them as my engineering execution. Conversely, I do not transfer my final operating-claim, customer-correction, incident-stop, or exception-decision responsibilities to Daniela.

6. Development status: December remains open

Owen’s and Ines’s October–December Q4 development focuses remain open through the required December cycle.

Owen’s focus is to continue demonstrating timely measurement preparation, explicit denominators and exact through-dates, early owner certification, and disciplined complete-or-incomplete exception closure. Ines’s focus is to produce one independent lifecycle-risk explanation in each required monthly cycle, distinguish routine non-state-changing work from escalation, and identify governed-state or audience risk without changing release behavior outside her authority.

October and November examples demonstrate progress; they are not completion of the full October–December cycle. The December cycle still needs to be completed and reviewed. No December development outcome is being pre-judged, and no development result changes either person’s authority, completes the focus early, or transfers an owner lane to me.

7. Next-cycle focus

1. Keep consequential decisions bounded by explicit caps, stop conditions, owners, reversibility, and evidence windows; do not let a clean operating read become an unapproved expansion or claim.
2. Complete and review the required December Q4 development cycle for Owen and Ines without pre-judging the outcomes or collapsing their separate lanes into my role.
3. Continue the quarterly one-lane evidence recheck after routine closure without creating a second approval queue or reopening owner closure.
4. Keep denominator, exact coverage dates, source freshness, named-owner certification, final-route reconciliation, exception status, and outcome-window maturity visible before operating or executive claims.
5. Leave routine owner-ready work with Owen, Ines, and Daniela while taking only the defined exception, correction, incident-stop, state-changing, and final-claim decisions that belong to my role.
6. Treat the live Helio Start batch and fifth-consumer reminder as bounded operational work until their permitted evidence windows support a different conclusion; do not infer maturity from clean controls alone.

Calibration note

This revision is decision-led. It credits Priya’s batch approval, Daniela’s November 1 launch authorization and reliability/release work, Owen’s measurement and exception work, Ines’s lifecycle-governance and message-state work, and Customer Success’s paid-active, support, and staffing work. It keeps those execution lanes distinct from my decision and claim responsibilities; preserves the four-lane evidence framing and explicit exclusions; calls the current paid batch live operational work rather than mature evidence; identifies the incomplete-setup reminder as the fifth shared-state consumer; and leaves the October–December development outcomes open through the December cycle.

arguments.title: Contractor Work Instructions — Campaign-Owner Evidence and Suppression-Check Preparation
arguments.body:
CONTRACTOR WORK INSTRUCTIONS
Campaign-owner evidence inventory and suppression-check preparation
Kickoff date: 2025-01-15

Purpose

Prepare a reliable evidence package for Helio’s campaign-owner and suppression-check decisions. The contractor’s role is evidence preparation: inventory what exists, identify what is missing or ambiguous, and draft repeatable checklists. The contractor does not assign campaign authority, approve records, certify campaigns as releasable, or exercise any decision rights held by Ines, Riley, or Daniela.

Decision-rights boundary

The contractor MAY:
- Locate and catalog existing campaign-owner evidence and suppression-check records.
- Record the source, date, scope, status, and limitations of each item.
- Identify the four campaign-owner gaps already reported as undocumented.
- Identify the six routine-template suppression-check records that are missing or lack repeatable written evidence.
- Compare available evidence against the agreed checklist requirements.
- Mark an item as present, missing, ambiguous, stale, conflicting, or not applicable, with supporting citations.
- Draft and test neutral checklist language and propose a consistent evidence format.
- Prepare questions and decision packets for Helio’s accountable owners.

The contractor MUST NOT:
- Assign, nominate, or change a campaign owner or campaign authority.
- Treat an evidence gap as permission to appoint an owner or act as the owner.
- Approve, backdate, reconstruct, or certify any suppression-check record.
- Decide that a campaign, template, or message is releasable, blocked, or approved for release.
- Resolve conflicting ownership or release evidence by choosing one party.
- Send, schedule, activate, or materially edit campaign messages or suppression controls.
- Represent the contractor’s checklist review as legal, compliance, lifecycle, or release approval.
- Inherit, substitute for, or make decisions reserved to Ines, Riley, or Daniela.
- Close a gap merely because an owner has been suggested or a checklist has been drafted.

Operating rule

A prepared artifact is not an approval. Use the labels “evidence found,” “evidence missing,” “evidence ambiguous,” “evidence stale,” “evidence conflicting,” and “decision required.” Do not use “approved,” “certified,” “owner assigned,” “releasable,” or “ready to send” unless the existing Helio decision owner has made and recorded that decision through the normal process.

Workstream 1: Inventory the four undocumented campaign-owner gaps

1. Start with the supplied campaign and template list. Preserve campaign IDs, names, channels, audiences, and source labels exactly as provided; do not normalize identifiers.
2. For each gap, search the designated Helio sources for evidence of accountable ownership, such as an approved brief, operating record, launch record, or other established source of truth.
3. Record each search and result in the evidence register. A blank result means “not found in the searched sources,” not “no owner exists.”
4. Where evidence is found, transcribe the evidence and its scope without interpreting it as a new assignment.
5. Where sources disagree, create a conflict entry listing each source and escalate the conflict. Do not choose a winner.
6. Where evidence is absent, create a decision item for the existing Helio owner. Do not populate an owner field with the contractor, a proposed person, or a guessed team.

Required campaign-owner evidence-register fields

- Gap ID
- Campaign/template ID and exact name
- Channel and audience/scope
- Source system, document, or record
- Source URL or durable locator
- Evidence date and last-updated date, if available
- Wording that identifies authority or accountability (quote or precise field)
- Scope covered by the evidence
- Evidence status: present / missing / ambiguous / stale / conflicting / not applicable
- Search date and sources checked
- Evidence limitations
- Decision required from Helio
- Routed-to accountable owner or forum, if already established
- Contractor preparer and preparation date

Do not enter a person as campaign owner in the register unless an existing Helio source already records that person as the accountable owner. If no accountable owner is documented, leave the decision field open and flag it for Helio ownership resolution.

Workstream 2: Inventory the six missing suppression-check records

1. Use the six routine templates identified in the kickoff scope as the fixed review set.
2. For each template, locate the existing suppression-check record or the established source where the check should be recorded.
3. Capture what was actually documented. Do not infer that a check occurred from a clean output, a later send, a prior template, or a verbal statement.
4. Mark the record missing when no contemporaneous or otherwise accepted record is located in the approved sources.
5. Mark the record ambiguous when a record exists but does not establish the required check, scope, date, checker, inputs, result, or exception handling.
6. Mark the record stale when it does not cover the relevant audience, send, or current suppression conditions according to the applicable Helio standard.
7. Preserve conflicting records as conflicts and route them for decision. Do not merge, rewrite, or certify them.
8. For each missing or inadequate record, prepare a proposed checklist and a clearly labeled “record to be completed by Helio” shell. The shell is a preparation aid, not a completed control record.

Minimum repeatable suppression-check checklist draft

The contractor may prepare a checklist containing these prompts:
- Template/campaign ID and exact version
- Intended send or activation date/time
- Audience definition and source
- Suppression inputs and source locations
- Required exclusion categories
- Date/time the check was run
- Person or system that performed the check
- Result and relevant counts or output reference
- Exceptions, overrides, or unresolved anomalies
- Remediation and retest reference, if applicable
- Evidence locator and retention location
- Helio decision owner’s review/approval field
- Final release decision field, left blank for Helio

The contractor may improve wording, ordering, and usability of this checklist after a dry run. The contractor may not fill the Helio review, approval, release, exception-acceptance, or certification fields.

Evidence handling and quality rules

- Cite the original source for every factual claim.
- Preserve timestamps, versions, and exact identifiers.
- Distinguish “not found” from “not done.”
- Distinguish “record missing” from “check failed.”
- Distinguish a proposed checklist from a completed suppression-check record.
- Do not manufacture dates, counts, checker names, approvals, or release status.
- Do not backfill a record from memory or from a downstream outcome.
- If access is unavailable, record “not accessible,” name the blocked source, and route the access request; do not treat inaccessible evidence as missing.
- Keep a change log for checklist revisions and identify who made each revision.

Handoff package for each gap

Deliver one evidence packet per campaign-owner gap and one per suppression-check template containing:
1. Scope and exact identifier.
2. Evidence register entries and source links/locators.
3. Search log, including sources checked and dates.
4. Findings labeled with the allowed evidence status.
5. Open questions and conflicts.
6. Draft repeatable checklist, if applicable.
7. A decision-request section with blanks for the existing Helio decision owner.
8. Change log and contractor preparer/date.

Decision-request format

Decision required: [state the unresolved issue without proposing an unauthorized decision]
Evidence available: [cite records]
Evidence missing or conflicting: [cite gaps]
Impact/urgency: [factual operational context only]
Options for Helio owner consideration: [only if requested; do not recommend by authority]
Decision owner: [existing Helio owner/forum; do not assign one]
Decision: [blank]
Decision date: [blank]
Release/certification status: [blank]

Helio ownership and release decisions

The existing Helio decision owners retain exclusive responsibility for:
- Assigning or confirming campaign authority and accountable owners.
- Determining whether an evidence gap is acceptable, must be remediated, or blocks work.
- Defining the authoritative suppression-check standard and any exceptions.
- Completing, accepting, rejecting, or certifying suppression-check records.
- Deciding whether a campaign or template is releasable.
- Approving, holding, changing, or cancelling a release.
- Resolving conflicts and recording the final rationale.
- Exercising the decision rights that remain with Ines, Riley, and Daniela.

The contractor should route completed packets through the established Helio channel. Routing a packet is not approval, and receipt by a decision owner does not mean the contractor has been delegated authority.

Completion criteria for the contractor

The preparation work is complete when:
- All four campaign-owner gaps have an evidence-register entry and a source search log.
- All six suppression-check templates have a status, cited evidence or a documented search result, and limitations.
- Every missing, ambiguous, stale, or conflicting item has an open decision item.
- Draft checklists are repeatable and versioned, with Helio decision fields blank.
- No campaign authority, approval, certification, release status, or exception decision has been assigned by the contractor.
- The handoff packet makes clear which questions Helio must decide.

A packet is not complete merely because all fields are filled. Blank decision fields and explicit unresolved classifications are correct outputs when Helio’s decision has not yet been made.

arguments.body:
December 8 Review Aid — Owen and Ines Q4 Development Evidence

Prepared for tomorrow’s review; snapshot closed December 7, 2027
Status: neutral evidence summary; formal judgment reserved for the December 8 meeting

Purpose and review guardrails

This aid organizes the complete October–December cycle evidence against the approved development focuses. It records observed work, handling of uncertainty, and authority boundaries without assigning a formal rating or conclusion in advance. The evidence reflects the owners’ execution; it does not transfer Riley’s decision, exception, disputed-semantics, customer-correction, incident-stop, state-changing, or final-claim responsibilities.

Approved focus 1 — Owen: measurement preparation and disciplined exception closure

Focus: Demonstrate timely measurement preparation; make denominators and exact through-dates visible; obtain owner certification; and close each cycle as complete only when the required inputs and definitions are certified and reconciled. If not, keep the status explicitly incomplete rather than substituting stale data or silently declaring success.

Three-cycle evidence:

• October: Exception synthesis identified a source-certification delay. The synthesis remained visibly incomplete until certified inputs arrived.
• November: Exception synthesis correctly reported no exception.
• December: Exception synthesis identified a source-certification delay. The synthesis remained visibly incomplete until certified inputs arrived.

Across the three syntheses, no missing field was concealed and no disputed semantic was silently resolved or relabeled. The exception descriptions distinguished source-certification delay from missing input, cross-surface discrepancy, disputed semantics, and no exception.

Authority boundary: Owen’s lane covers measurement preparation, definitions, denominator and unit clarity, routine source completeness, named-owner certification tracking, and exception reporting. His work does not authorize a causal or executive claim, readiness conclusion, disputed-semantic resolution, revenue or pipeline treatment, forecast credit, board language, or a broader operating decision.

Review prompts: Was the evidence prepared and updated in time for each cycle? Were denominators, coverage dates, certifications, and status visibility adequate? Did the complete/incomplete distinction remain accurate when certification was delayed? Were the exception categories applied consistently across cycles?

Approved focus 2 — Ines: independent lifecycle-risk explanation and appropriate escalation

Focus: Produce one independent lifecycle-risk explanation in each required monthly cycle; distinguish routine non-state-changing work from state-changing or otherwise consequential proposals; identify governed-state or audience risk; and escalate before release when the matter exceeds existing authority, without changing trigger, audience, message state, or release behavior outside that authority.

Three-cycle evidence:

• October–December: Three lifecycle-risk explanations covered seven routine, non-state-changing items and two state-changing proposals.
• Routine items: The seven routine items were handled within the existing lifecycle-governance and send-authority lane.
• State-changing proposals: Both proposals were escalated to Riley before release. No release occurred under Ines’s routine authority in place of the escalation.

The evidence describes risk identification and routing; it does not treat escalation as approval, nor does it imply that a state-changing proposal was authorized or shipped. No authority expansion, lifecycle bypass, audience broadening, or transfer of final decision or claim authority is inferred.

Authority boundary: Ines’s lane covers lifecycle governance, message-state controls, owner-state certification, suppression and stop behavior, and routine non-state-changing lifecycle releases within existing send authority. State-changing, high-risk, exception-heavy, or otherwise consequential matters remain subject to escalation and the applicable decision owner.

Review prompts: Did each cycle contain an independent lifecycle-risk explanation? Were routine and state-changing matters distinguished correctly? Did the explanations identify governed-state or audience risk clearly? Were both state-changing proposals escalated before release, with no out-of-lane release or authority expansion?

Cross-focus evidence and limits

• Both focuses show repeated cycle evidence rather than a single favorable example: three Owen syntheses and three Ines explanations.
• The evidence supports review of process execution, status integrity, risk recognition, and escalation behavior. It does not by itself establish customer impact, lifecycle performance, institutional effectiveness, or mature business outcomes.
• A source-certification delay is not equivalent to a failure when the work remains visibly incomplete and closes only after certification; likewise, a no-exception cycle is not a broader readiness or claim decision.
• Escalation demonstrates preservation of the authority boundary; it is not itself approval or evidence that the proposed change should be released.
• Riley’s formal judgment, including any conclusion about development-focus completion or performance, is reserved for the December 8 review meeting.

Meeting use

1. Confirm the evidence for each monthly cycle against the approved focus language.
2. Separate observed execution from interpretation and formal judgment.
3. Check that authority limits remained unchanged: routine owner work stayed with the owner; state-changing proposals were escalated before release.
4. Record the formal judgment only during the December 8 review.

arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft

Review context

Priya opened the 2027 self-review window on November 8, 2027, with a first-draft deadline of November 19. This revision is decision-led: it starts with the consequential choices I made, states the evidence and limits behind each choice, and then credits the people who executed their own lanes. It does not treat preparation as approval, operating control as customer outcome, or another person’s execution as my own.

1. Decisions I made and the boundaries I held

My central contribution in 2027 was to make consequential decisions explicit, bounded, reversible, and evidence-aware. I owned the high-stakes decision and final-claim boundary: exception decisions, disputed semantics, cross-surface consequences, customer corrections, incident stops, state-changing or exception-heavy matters, causal and executive-language decisions, revenue and forecast treatment, board readiness, and final operating claims.

I did not own routine source preparation, routine measurement closure, routine lifecycle execution, engineering release execution, or rollback execution. I did not turn a clean operating read into a broader authorization, and I did not claim that a decision I made meant I had performed the underlying owner work.

The year-end evidence framing remained four separate lanes:

1. Helio Start — customer-outcome and operating-control evidence, with organic and paid-source evidence kept separate.
2. Expansion Assist — descriptive evidence for the governed population, retaining its own eligibility definition, exposure denominator, treatment, outcome window, exclusions, and maturity status.
3. Pricing-page path quality and continuity — post-rollout continuity evidence, including sessions, flow starts, admission completion, support-time measures, coverage dates, and metric definitions.
4. CS auto-nudge system controls — system-control evidence covering governed decisions, field-specific holds, freshness and conflict handling, visible outcomes, corrections, disagreements, incidents, monitoring, release, and rollback.

Each lane retained its own denominator, coverage dates, outcome window, exclusions, source-as-of time, reliability evidence, and maturity limits. The incomplete-setup reminder was the fifth shared-state production consumer, not a sixth evidence lane. Its operation stayed within the established boundaries and did not create a reusable audience, broader entitlement, new consumer authority, or transfer of an owner lane.

2. Decision: approve and operate one bounded Helio Start paid-search batch

Decision and my role

I prepared and maintained the bounded Helio Start paid-search proposal and owned its operating boundaries and claim limits. The design was one approved high-intent batch only, closing at the earlier of $8,000 in cumulative paid-source spend or 25 admitted workspaces. Existing eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, freshness, hold, suppression, instrumentation, dedupe, assisted-routing, correction, and incident-stop rules remained unchanged. No additional paid batch was included or implied.

The proposal also preserved explicit stop and pause conditions: stop on an unsupported admission; pause if paid-source attribution could not reconcile from eligibility-flow start through the final route; and, after at least 10 admissions, pause if more than 10% of admitted workspaces exceeded 90 account-level support minutes. The batch did not create a pipeline target or treatment, forecast credit, revenue claim, eligibility change, lifecycle bypass, scale claim, or permission to infer authority from remaining spend or admissions capacity.

Evidence used for the decision

The certified Q2 evidence used to support the constrained decision was descriptive operating evidence: 18 of 25 workspaces were paid-active; refund-adjusted collected cash was $27,860; median account-level support effort was 33 minutes; p90 effort was 116 minutes; and 5 of 25 workspaces exceeded 90 minutes. These inputs supported a bounded operating decision. They were not randomized or causal acquisition evidence and did not establish mature retention, acquisition economics, pipeline contribution, forecast performance, or results for the new cohort.

Explicit credits

Priya approved the budget and the bounded batch. Her approval was the separate budget-and-batch decision; it was not a waiver of the operating boundaries and did not authorize a second batch.

Daniela separately completed the November 1 launch authorization after verifying the launch-day proofs: current attribution endpoints and end-to-end reconciliation; production release, enablement, cap enforcement, audit logging, and rollback controls; and staffed Customer Success owner-and-backup coverage for Monday–Friday, 8:00am–6:00pm Central, with after-hours cases routed to the next service opening. I credit Daniela’s launch authorization and technical/reliability work separately from my proposal and decision-boundary work.

Owen owned the refund-adjusted collected-cash evidence and the measurement/denominator work. Customer Success owned paid-active status, account-level support evidence, staffing, and the staffed handoff. December 8 Review Aid — Owen and Ines Q4 Development Evidence

Prepared for tomorrow’s review; snapshot closed December 7, 2027
